  • According to recent reports, work, kids, family obligations, running your household, a hobby if you’re lucky enough to have time for one — all of these things take time and energy.
  • Even when you’ve been married for years, once you and your partner get in a routine of not having sex, it can feel awkward or strange to try and start it up again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s all about easing in (and examining what got you here.).

According to recent reports, work, kids, family obligations, running your household, a hobby if you’re lucky enough to have time for one — all of these things take time and energy. It’s enough to have you laid out on the couch, carcass style, at the end of a regular day. When something actually goes wrong, like the kids get sick or a work project keeps you at your desk late, it’s even harder to imagine getting it up at the end of the day. No matter how much you love your spouse, sex droughts come for everyone at some point (ahem, many points) throughout a relationship. If it’s been a while and you want to get back in the game, here’s how to reinitiate.

Even when you’ve been married for years, once you and your partner get in a routine of not having sex, it can feel awkward or strange to try and start it up again. It almost feels like you have to acknowledge the drought, and therefore the bad things that led up to it, or perhaps the parts you’ve both played in letting it drag on. It’s just a lot, but try not to blame yourself.

According to recent reports, “Sex droughts are far more common than pop culture would have us believe. They're certainly nothing to be ashamed of, nor do they represent a ‘failure,’” states Angie Rowntree, ABS, board-certified sexologist and founder and filmmaker behind the award-winning ethical adult film site Sssh.com. “Life happens. Bodies get sick or injured, or may have different needs. Children are born and demand your time and care. Older parents may need care. Jobs might change. Any number of stresses and interruptions in your life can upend what was your regularly scheduled Saturday date night or sap you of the carefree mojo you’d usually bring to the bedroom. None of that is a shortcoming, or is anyone’s fault.”.

Sources indicate that every couple is different in terms of how much sex is enough for them to feel happy with it, so remember that you don’t have to meet some made-up quota of intimate evenings per week. If you are ready to get back into the groove, though, here’s how to start.

First, initiating sex after a long break comes with natural stress and pressure. If it doesn’t land with your spouse, don’t let it get you down.

It has been revealed that “Sometimes we need a little warm-up before we get back in the saddle, so to speak. Start small. Don’t hint with memes, but act. Physical touch and flirtation are things that ignite foreplay in the mind. Kiss for a little longer than usual before you leave. Send a suggestive text during the day. Get into bed and cuddle, but without immediately reaching below the belt. You’re essentially reminding each other that you still desire each other,” Rowntree says.

It’s also totally OK to address the elephant in the room, Rowntree claims. Tell your partner, “I miss being close to you. Can we make some time tonight?” This way you’re giving them an invitation and creating a little anticipation all at once.

If you go for it and your partner turns you down, don’t turn a situational no into a personal one, says Rowntree.

It has been revealed that “When they say, ‘Honey, I’m tired,’ it becomes, ‘You don’t turn me on anymore.’ The longer you’ve been together, the more history there can be attached to that moment. If one person is usually initiating sex, or usually declining it, those long-term behavior patterns can make a huge impact.”.

If there’s longstanding angst in your relationship around who initiates and how often, that in and of itself can lead to more sex droughts. It’s something to have a “frank discussion” about, Rowntree advises. During that conversation, you want to figure out how to separate “I don’t want sex right now” from “I don’t want you.”.

Sources indicate that “You want to frame your communication in a way that maintains your partner’s desirability and your interest. For instance: ‘I’m exhausted tonight, but can we cuddle?’ or, ‘Why don’t I wake you up and we can take a shower together tomorrow morning before I have to go?’ The point is, you’re declining the timing, not rejecting your partner, or giving them any ambiguity about your attraction to them.”.

If challenges around initiating are keeping you two on a holding pattern sex-wise, again, talk about it. Find a time when you have privacy and are fully clothed so there’s no immediate pressure, and hash out the details of each other’s wants, needs, and preferences around initiating. Rowntree states you should ask each other:.

“Sometimes it really is the little things that turn a ‘meh, maybe’ into a spark that goes all the way. Also, please stop feeling like you need elaborate Instagram-worthy seduction schemes. There’s no reason to overcomplicate basic human desire. Put on music and pour a drink together after work. Send a flirty text before you get home. Give them a lingering kiss in the kitchen that morning. Or just say, ‘Why don’t we go to bed early tonight? I’ve missed you.’”.

#79385. Industry News: The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

📅 09 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (753 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: The Real Reason We Struggle With Screen Time

📅 09 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (753 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, how should we all tackle phone use and screen time?
  • Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?
  • Recent findings suggest that I don’t see much evidence of it out there.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, how should we all tackle phone use and screen time? An ancient Eleusinian mystery may hold the answer.

Does anyone have a truly healthy relationship with their phone?

Recent findings suggest that I don’t see much evidence of it out there. Personally, the phone is undeniably useful but still feels like a foreign object in my hand — a feeling that was brought into stark relief the second my kids were old enough to pick up a screen. To them, a tablet or phone offers an enticing, comforting, and even productive space. Not healthy, exactly, but familiar. For me, it’s alien — and ground zero for a cultural battle against brain rot, attention loss, and reality itself. Phones stress me out.

I ran into a much needed perspective on this dilemma in a long, thoughtful essay by Karl Ove Knausgaard, the brilliant Norwegian writer with an uncanny ability to see the world as it is, in meticulous detail. My struggle, as he helped me to see, comes from those most influential years in my life — the years before the smartphone. “To understand a man, you have to know what was happening in the world when he was twenty, Napoleon is supposed to have remarked,” writes Knausgaard in Harper’s Magazine. “The quotation is probably apocryphal, but that doesn’t mean it’s not true.”.

It has been revealed that my Napoleonic prime was in the 2000s — shortly after the advent of Facebook, but right before the iPhone was in everyone’s hands. For Knausgaard, who is 56 years old, the internet barely existed in his twenties. He admits that he has been ignoring the fundamental influences of such technological advances since. “Not once in those forty years have I turned my attention to technology and tried to understand it,” Knausgaard writes, “how it works in itself, how it works in me. It’s as if I had moved to a foreign country and not bothered to learn its language, as if I am content with not understanding what is happening around me and just settling for my own little world. This lately feels like serious neglect.”.

In a recent development, this resonates. While I spend considerable time trying to understand and control the impacts of screen time on my kids' developing brains, I hardly pay attention to my own use. What am I doing when I check for emails, Slack messages, and texts with lab rat-like repetition, or scroll Reddit News and The Upcoming York Times at every down moment, or get lost in Instagram and YouTube rabbit holes? More importantly, what should I do about it?

Knausgaard found his technological insight by heading out to Athens, Greece to talk to James Bridle, an author and artist with a specialty in nonhuman ways of thinking (and what orangutans can teach us about politics). In a sense, Bridle sees technology as getting in the way of experience. Sounding like a free range parenting proselytizer, he states that “the only thing you can do is experience it and do it yourself. You have to do it, you have to experience it, it has to happen to you. Bodily, physically — because you’re part of the world.”.

In a recent development, bridle takes this deeper, offering the example of an ancient Eleusinian cult in which initiates were led into a dark room, shown a “whirlwind of impressions, without anyone telling them what they were seeing or what it meant” and being left to interpret that on their own. The next year, they were shown the initiation from the outside, “and you could say that only then, when the gaze from within was complemented by the gaze from without, was the initiation completed.”.

Industry observers note that this metaphor for the digital world made it all click for me. We’re all too often inside looking at the whirlwind of the internet with little control and understanding. There are more of us now trying to step outside of this world — to see the puppet masters at play in order to walk away from it all.

In a recent development, we’re not going back to 2006, that innocent year before the iPhone was introduced. And I don’t think that should be the goal. The technology that has been introduced since my childhood is incredible, powerful, and a big piece of human progress. But it’s no replacement for the real world lessons I get when I put down the phone and experience life, unfiltered.

21 Thanksgiving Table Scripts For The Relative Who Always Starts Sh*t

💡 Key Takeaways
  • “I didn’t know people I knew held these types of views” is a zinger.
  • It happens every year but it never gets less jarring.
  • There’s nothing worse than when that one pot-stirring family member crosses you and you immediately feel your temper flare red hot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I didn’t know people I knew held these types of views” is a zinger.

It happens every year but it never gets less jarring. That one drunk uncle brings up politics (and never in a thoughtful way). Your mother-in-law asks about that one sensitive subject that’s really none of her business. Your grandma comments on how much food is on your teen daughter’s plate. Whatever the topic, family gatherings have a way of bringing a bunch of people with differing opinions around one table, where they’re just comfortable enough with everyone to spew their hot takes and outdated perspectives. If you have someone like this in your family, here are some Thanksgiving table scripts to respond to that one relative who always starts sh*t.

There’s nothing worse than when that one pot-stirring family member crosses you and you immediately feel your temper flare red hot. Or you get completely flustered and fumble for words. When someone pushes a boundary of yours, take a beat before responding.

“Pause, take a breath, and press your feet into the ground to feel a bit more grounded. Give yourself permission to slow down and stay in your body so you don't feel pressured to keep answering or discussing something you're not comfortable with. You don't owe anyone at the dinner table answers you aren't comfortable giving,” claims Chloë Bean, LMFT, a somatic trauma therapist in Los Angeles.

You’re not alone in feeling like the holidays are a hotbed for family conflict, experts say.

“Perhaps things start off great, but after a few rounds of seasonal cocktails, Uncle So-and-So and Grandma Such-and-Such start spouting off some out-of-pocket sh*t. This has only increased as our socio-political climate intensifies and the gap between generational understandings widens,” claims Whitney Polich, LICSW, licensed clinical social worker. “Despite this happening every year, perhaps we are still a bit gobsmacked and unsure of what to say, until the drive home when the perfect clapback comes to mind.”.

Whether you clap back in the moment and escalate or would rather de-escalate, practicing a few responses in your head (or even in the mirror) ahead of the gathering can help you stay grounded and protect your peace.

There are three genres of response you could go with here, claims Ashley Hamm, LPC, a licensed professional counselor who specializes in anxiety and people-pleasing.

According to recent reports, “Sometimes acting surprised or baffled is enough to throw someone off-kilter and get them off the subject. This is especially useful if someone is sharing something problematic that they might know deep down is inappropriate to share,” notes Hamm.

Try these: “I’m surprised you feel comfortable sharing ideas like that.” “I have no idea what you are talking about.” “I’m surprised to hear you say that; I didn’t know people I knew held these types of views.”.

Keep a few alternate subjects in the back of your mind in case you need a quick diversion — a conversational smoke bomb, if you will.

Think: “Speaking of the news, I saw a really funny story about…” “Speaking of the news, I saw a really heartwarming story about…” “I’d rather not talk about our opinions on that because I don’t get to see you very often, and I’d rather hear about what you’ve been up to personally!”.

“Simply acting like you didn’t hear them is a great strategy to stay disentangled from sensitive or divisive topics. Using some of the changing topics ideas above, you can simply start a new topic, or respond to the most recent unproblematic thing someone said,” Hamm notes.

For example: “Oh, Aunt Mary, you were just talking about your recipe for the green bean casserole. I’d love to hear more about where you found it.” “Hmm, not sure what to say to that. Anyways, I’ve been trying to watch more movies lately. Has anyone seen anything good?”.

Bookmark ‘em for your family’s Thanksgiving and thank yourself later.

For those genuinely looking for their baby's name to stand out, you might want to try something stunning and standalone like Elspeth or Mamie. If those tickle your fancy, keep reading for a compilation of names with an unusual quality that's elegant, edgy, and will surely stand the test of time.

Recent findings suggest that agatha is a very unique option for little girls these days, but it wasn’t always! It stayed in the top 1000 baby names from 1900 to 1945, and hasn’t been seen since. The name Agatha means “good” or “honorable,” which is such a powerful meaning for your little one.

According to recent reports, although it peaked in the nation’s top 100 names in 1880, Agnes fell off the charts sometime in the ‘70s. But the Greek name, which means “pure,” is poised for a comeback. The nickname Aggie, in particular,” has loads of retro charm.

From the 1880s until around the early 1930s, Alma held tight in the top 100 names for girls in the United States. It dropped pretty dramatically in the late ‘90s and early ‘00s and has settled just inside of the top 1000. A name with origins in many cultures, it means “nourishing” or “soul.”.

It has been revealed that this elegant name started strong in the 1800s, tapered off, shot to its peak in the late 1960s, and has gradually waned in popularity since. Of British and French origin, it means “noble strength.”.

Latin for “venerable” or “majestic,” Augusta is grand in all the right ways. It has major great-aunt-who’s-traveled-the-world energy. Huge selling point: Gussie is an unbearably cute nickname.

It has been revealed that barbara is a classic in every sense of the word, and it definitely has an old-fashioned feel. The name Barbara means “foreign” or “strange,” and was most popular from the ‘20s through the ‘60s. You can use Barbie, Babs, or Barb as a cute nickname, too.

Bernie is the absolute cutest girl nickname, and the name Bernadette really sells it. This old-fashioned choice means “brave bear” or “strong,” and it was most popular in the 1920s.

An oldie but a goodie of a Greek name, Beryl means “light green semiprecious gemstone” and is perfect for the baby girl who’s the jewel of your eye.

A feminine name of Hebrew origin, Beulah means “bride.” That might make you think of how fast your daughter will grow up, but look at it like this — that’s a long way off, and it’s something to look forward to when it eventually arrives. Although this name was ranked #123 for girls in the U.S. in 1880, it’s dropped to the #6000-ish range today.

You’d think this name would have seen a bigger resurgence recently with so much love for The Golden Girls! But Blanche, a French name meaning “white” or “pure,” currently sits at #11,298 in popularity for U.S. girl names. For context, it was a top 100 name in the 1880s.

It has been revealed that never a wildly common name, Cicely hovered around the #5,000 mark through most of the early 1900s before dropping to its current ranking of #11,351 for girls. It means “blind of self-beauty.”.

Sources indicate that the feminine version of Claude, the name Claudette means “lame,” which isn’t all that great — but at least it’s French! It also hasn’t been popular since 1973, so you know she’ll be the only one in her preschool class.

Although Cordelia fell out of favor a little in the late ‘90s, it’s been slowly creeping back up the charts. And why not? This lovely name of Latin origin has the sweetest meaning: “heart.”.

This lovely name means “steadfast,” which is exactly what you want your kid to be (except maybe at bedtime!). It feels a little prim, sure, but you could also soften it up by calling her Connie.

It has been revealed that this beautiful name is an elaborate form of Cora. It means “little heart,” which perfectly describes your little one. It’s also forever tied to Coretta Scott King, the civil rights leader who carried her husband’s legacy forward for decades.

While the name has had some recent traction thanks to Selling Sunset’s Davina Potratz, it’s a fairly uncommon sweet name that means “beloved” — a sweet nod to your beloved bundle of joy.

Industry observers note that from the Greek word delphís, this beautiful baby name means “dolphin” — and how cute is that? The name is also derived from Delphi, the home of an oracle in Greek mythology. It at the moment ranks #3643 for girl names in the U.S.

According to recent reports, oh goodness, imagine a sweet little baby named Dorothea! It’s just too much. This moniker means “gift of God” and has Greek origins. You can choose nicknames like Thea or Dottie, too, and hasn’t been on the popular chart since 1970.

According to recent reports, it’s surprising that this name ranks all the way down at #15927 on the list because it’s really freaking cute! Meaning “sweet, candy,” Dulcie is related to Dulce — the name that inspired Cervantes’ Dulcinea, Don Quixote’s chosen lady.

It has been revealed that want your baby girl to stand strong in her voice? Consider this name, which means “well-spoken” (and happens to be the name of the tough and tenacious Effie White from Dreamgirls). Although Effie ranked #63 in the 1880s, it sits at #2120 today.

I love the simplicity of Ellen. It’s so sweet and lovely, and conjures up images of girls being badasses while also being little dollops of joy — sugar and spice and everything nice. Ellen means “torch” or “bright light” and was in the top 100 of baby girl names for literal decades. Now, it sits at #920.

A strong and sturdy name of Hebrew and Scottish origin, Elspeth means “chosen by God.” While it hasn’t made much headway outside of the U.K., it has a childish charm that might be fit for a sweet comeback.

In a recent development, is Ethel not the absolute sweetest? This name just brings such joy, and its meaning is “noble.” The last time it hit the popularity charts was in the ‘70s, so I think it’s definitely time to bring back this old-fashioned cutie.

This unique name of Greek origin is perfect for your little one as it means “generous gift.” It also stems from Greek mythology, giving off some goddess vibes, too.

Like Effie, this Greek name means “well-spoken,” but it also means “sweetly speaking” — and, well, that just sounds lovely. Eulalia has a soft, earthy appeal, too, as it’s the name of a tall green grass that grows in Eastern Asia.

Faye had a good run of popularity in the ‘30s, but otherwise hasn’t come close to that same acclaim. It’s still unique now, but I suspect that the fantasy book culture has brought Faye — which means “fairy” or “belief” — back into the fold.

Industry observers note that don't underestimate this name that you might associate with your great-aunt! Meaning "strength of a spear," the German moniker feels a bit flinty but has a cute, much softer nickname in Gertie.

Sources indicate that this Welsh name means “land nation,” but it has a quaint and sweet sound to it that defies its definition. And of course, there’s the Motown legend Gladys Knight, which makes it even more legendary.

In a recent development, henri, Etta, Rett — so many sweet nicknames can come from the name Henrietta. It hasn’t been on the popular lists since 1968, and Henrietta also means “home ruler.”.

A form of Esther, Hester means “star.” And whatever, no one cares about the Hester Prynne baggage. In fact, that kind of makes this name even cooler. A heroine who refused to be shamed into submission? Heck yeah.

An abbreviated form of Katherine, this sweet name means "pure." Naturally, it's a purr-fect name for cat lovers. It's also been the name of many famous characters, from Kitty Bennet of Pride and Prejudice to Kitty Pryde of X-Men.

In Roman mythology, Lavinia was the wife of Aeneas and the namesake of an ancient city, so this comes with a bit of historical pedigree. It’s lush and lyrical, not fussy at all, and the nickname Vinnie is so unexpectedly perfect for a little girl.

This lilting name of Hebrew and Arabic origin has beautiful (and sort of mysterious) meanings of “dark beauty” and “born at night.” If you grew up obsessed with Anna Sewell’s classic novel Black Beauty, this could be the old-fashioned girl’s name for your little one.

In a recent development, if you love Haunted Mansion, you undoubtedly know Madame Leota. So, while this name is pretty uncommon (#14,360 for girls’ names in the U.S.), it’s beloved in the Disney fan community. Germanic, it means “of the people.”.

According to recent reports, loretta means “laurel,” which has such a sweet, country vibe. Retta, Lo, Etta, Rettie — there are so many cute nickname options for this old-fashioned choice. In the 1910s and ‘20s, this name was always in the top 150, and then ended up in the top 100 for pretty much all of the ‘30s.

A lovely name that means “little and womanly,” Lottie is a diminutive of the French name Charlotte. It has a “je ne sais quoi” flair that is due for a comeback... especially with the popular characters of the same name from Disney’s The Princess and the Frog and Showtime’s Yellowjackets.

I just love this one so much — it sounds like a storybook character! The name Louise means “renowned warrior,” which is pretty amazing, and while it’s gaining some traction on the popularity charts, it’s still a unique choice. (It was most popular in the 1910s.).

How sweet is Mabel? The name literally means “lovable,” and while it has gotten more popular in recent years, it’s still a unique choice for your little one. Before 2013, it hadn’t been on the popular charts since 1964.

Thanks to Hilary Duff (or Parenthood fave Mae Whitman), this darling little moniker could make a comeback, but Mae is definitely still considered old-fashioned. It’s often a diminutive of names like Margaret or Mary, but it stands on its own very well. It’s just so spunky and cute. Mae also means “maiden” or “young woman” and was in the top 100 baby girl names from 1900 to 1920.

Sources indicate that maude is just so punchy, I’m obsessed. This cute old-fashioned girl name hasn’t been on the popularity charts since 1950, and it means “powerful in battle.” Hell yeah, girl!

This adorable name, a shorter version of Margaret or another form of Mary, was famously chosen by Meryl Streep for her daughter Mamie Gummer. It means “pearl” and “star of the sea,” both beautiful metaphors for your newly introduced treasure.

Midge stems from the Greek word for “pearl” — but you may better recognize it as the name of the title character in Prime Video’s hit series The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel. Although the name dropped off in popularity in the ‘70s, it’s making a gradual comeback, currently ranking #2603.

This elegant English name means “gentle strength” and encapsulates both maturity and tenderness, making it a fantastic choice for the well-rounded daughter you want to raise.

Millicent just sounds vintage right off the bat, and its popularity journey truly makes that case — it hasn’t been on the lists since 1965. You can go with Millie for a cute nickname, but I truly do think Millicent just sounds so cool. It also means “strong in work.”.

It has been revealed that who can forget Moaning Myrtle from Harry Potter? But this cute name has a richer history than that. Its origins come from the “evergreen shrub,” which was sacred to the goddess Venus as a symbol of love. So, in some ways, this name could symbolize your everlasting love for your baby girl.

Industry observers note that OK, this might be what you call your grandmother, but it has a cute ring to it, too. The Hebrew name, which means "grace," has a uniquely modern, feminine vibe that stands out.

Sources indicate that this gender-neutral name of Old Norse origins boasts many meanings: “wealth,” “honor,” “respect,” “man’s defender,” and “ancestor’s relic.” So, if you’re pretty sure your kid is destined to be a wild card, Ola it is! This name ranked in the top 200s during the 1880s, but today it has settled in around the #6800 mark.

Patricia feels incredibly traditional, but Patty for a little girl? Come on, we’ve got to bring it back. Patricia means “noble” and is a variant of Patrick if you like the Irish connection.

It has been revealed that doesn’t this just sound like it belongs to the main character of a cozy British mystery? Greek for “beloved,” it boasts a bunch of punchy nicknames like Mena, Pippa, and Pip.

OK, OK, bear with me — Prudence is extremely old-fashioned, but it also has the delightful nickname of Prue! Prudence means “wise,” “skilled,” or “intelligent,” and was extremely common during the Middle Ages. (It hasn’t been in the top 1000 baby girl names since 1948, either.).

Recent findings suggest that thanks to Dolly Parton’s immense popularity, the name Jolene has shot up the rankings in recent years. But this twangy name, which is a variant of Rae, is a much less common option (#10,919 for girl names in the U.S.) that offers the same spirit.

Recent findings suggest that calling all Ravenclaws! Harry Potter fans who call this house home will surely recognize Rowena as the first name of its founder. Outside of its HP claim to fame, the name means “famous friend” and “pure spear.” Plus, it comes with the cool nickname Ro.

It has been revealed that oh, Susannah! Don’t you cry for me! Whether you spell it Suzanna, Susanna, or with the traditional H at the end, this name is a classic. Susannah means “lily,” so it has a sweet, nature-related connection and a ton of cute nicknames, from Susie (or Suzie) to Suze and Anna. It was only in the top 1000 of baby girl names from 1967 to 1978, and even then, it was still one of the more unique options.

Thelma was popularized by the 1887 novel by Marie Corelli, and it means “will” in Greek. It’s peak grandma chic! And if you have two daughters, Thelma and Louise is right there. (Kidding... mostly.).

In a recent development, theodora is the feminine form of Theodore, meaning “gift of God.” It’s just so cute, and Theo is a darling name for a little girl (so is Teddy, honestly!). From 1954 to 2019, it didn’t even top the charts, but it’s making a slow comeback.

In a recent development, wilhelmina is just so gorgeous, and I love all of the nicknames you can pick for this one. The name also means “resolute protector,” so it feels like a strong moniker for your little gal. Bonus: It hasn’t been on the popularity charts since 1952, so you know it’s unique.

This lovely Welsh name means "blessed peace," which, sure, doesn't exactly align with everyone's favorite Winifred — the iconic red-haired witch from Hocus Pocus. But the name has a sophisticated feeling to it, and the nickname Winnie is just so delightful.

What 28 Years Later Can Tell Us About Men Today

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Danny Boyle’s zombie trilogy is a timely and notable meditation about masculinity.

According to recent reports, will it take a zombie apocalypse to fix masculinity? The thought occurred to me as I sat in a theater taking in Danny Boyle’s 28 Years Later the other day. This intense, gory, nudity-laden flick was also one of a surprisingly heartwarming journey for a young boy, Spike, who doesn’t buy into his community’s view of the world. Everyone around him is fearful, incurious, and readily accepts convenient and clear falsehoods about their lives. Spike seeks hope, even if it requires him to face the violent, cruel, and potentially fatal real world off his island.

Industry observers note that I won’t spoil too much in the way of the plot but I will say that the way the story speaks to masculinity — wading through lost men, toxic lies, and not-so-symbolic alpha males (in the form of one truly terrifying zombie) — is thoughtful and fresh. In context of the cultural landscape for boys and men today, it’s the kind of exploration we could really use.

Two months ago, Scott Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU and media tour de force affectionately known on his podcast as Prof G, took to The View to talk, as he does so often, about masculinity.

Industry observers note that “I like the idea of restoring an aspirational vision of masculinity,” he mentioned to a room that seemed, a bit surprisingly, in total agreement. “I don’t think there’s anything wrong with leaning into your femininity or masculinity if it feels natural.”.

In his view, this vision of masculinity involves three pillars: provider, procreator, and protector.

In 28 Years Later, Spike becomes the provider, chasing the health care his mom needs that his dad ignores.

Sources indicate that when it comes to the provider, “every man at the outset of his career should take economic responsibility for his household. Sometimes that means getting out of the way” of your more successful partner, he says, and other times it means stepping up. For procreation, he says we should channel “that fire of desire… the right ways [to] make you a better man — kinder, stronger, thinking about how you dress … showering, for God’s sake.”.

Finally, he indicates that in an aspirational vision of masculinity, “your default operating system is protection.” This is a more gentle and empathetic pillar than it might sound on its face. “A lot of women don’t feel safe on the subway,” he explains, “or they see men walking down the street, they cross the sidewalk.” This is due to men eschewing their duty as protector. And “it’s not just physical,” he continues. “When you see a group being demonized, your default setting as a man is you move to protection.”.

In 28 Years Later, Spike found himself chasing this view of masculinity headlong: providing the health care his mom needed that his dad would not, protecting her from zombies and himself from indoctrination, not exactly chasing procreation (he’s 12) but rejecting his father’s philandering example. The fact that he lives in a post-apocalyptic landscape in many senses brings clarity to his vision. When there are no worldly comforts, moral clarity arises.

It has been revealed that danny Boyle and Prof G have this in common: They’re both speaking to the broadest possible audiences about things that so many men primarily discuss with, well, other men. With 28 Years Later raking in over $100 million at the box office already and The View’s audience being, well, The View’s audience, it’s refreshing to see such discussion spilling out into the public.

Masculinity is making a comeback. It’s time to talk about it.

8 Essentials for Your Family's First Trip to Disney World

📅 03 Jan 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Moms

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com.
  • Recent findings suggest that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years.
  • She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Katie Leigh Matthews is a contributing writer for Moms.com. As the mom of a sweet and sensitive 9-year-old boy and a wild and free 5-year-old girl, she brings her ever-evolving experience of parenting to everything she writes.

Recent findings suggest that she’s been writing forever, and professionally for three years. With a degree in communications and a fascination for all things mental health, she seeks to uncover and share what genuinely helps us be more of who we are capable of being, especially with our kids. Towards that end, she writes often on introversion and the trait of high sensitivity to highlight their strengths and promote more self-compassion among all who share them. She regularly collaborates with experts in these fields to create content that informs, encourages, and empowers.

She loves that through Moms.com, she can put her chronic overthinking of every parenting decision to good use by saving readers time and hopefully a headache or two.

In a recent development, katie lives in Birmingham, Alabama, with her husband and two kids. On any given day she’s probably either rewatching her favorite highlights for the 100th time or dipping her toes in any creek she can find.

It has been revealed that you’ve booked your tickets. You’ve planned your itinerary. You’ve figured out the My Disney Experience App (you think.) You’re as ready as you can be for your family’s first trip to Disney World. Then it dawns on you: What do you need to pack? Shopping for essentials for your first family trip to Disney World is an art – it’s about knowing your family and what you all need to thrive on one of the most exciting, most magical, and yes, sometimes stressful family vacations.

In a recent development, A little online searching will rapidly convince you you'll need to buy extra luggage just to pack park essentials, but don’t stress. As an easily-overwhelmed mom who recently braved Disney World for the first time, I've got some hard-won advice to help guide your vacation prep and inform your packing list. Plus, I've scoured the internet for top picks of the most-used sanity-saving products to make the happiest place on earth live up to its name for you and your family.

Recent findings suggest that for many parents, taking the kids to Disney World at least once during their childhood is a bucket list goal. When that dream is finally realized, there is a mix of idyllic anticipation and anxious uncertainty. It’s not surprising that many parents find planning for a trip to Disney World to be a stressful experience.

Recent findings suggest that when it comes to Disney World, there are two types of parents: those who have fond memories of their own childhood Disney vacation, and those who hope to give their own kids the trip they didn’t get to experience growing up. Whichever type you are, the goal is the same: To give your kids a core-memory-making family vacation they’ll cherish forever. Of course, a love of Disney also evokes childhood nostalgia that is so fun to share with your own children. The legacy of classic and modern Disney characters, movies, and parks is a special thing to pass on to the next generation and something that carries a lot of weight for many.

Along with all the hopes and expectations wrapped up in a family trip to Disney World, the cost of the vacation only adds to the pressure to make it the best trip ever. For budget travelers, the average weeklong Disney World vacation for a family of four can cost $6,000 or more, according to NerdWallet, so ensuring you get your money’s worth is a huge factor. Not only that, but with so much to see, do, and experience in the parks, a vacation to Disney World is a complex trip to plan. Some families even turn to Disney vacation planners and travel agents to help with the sheer volume of logistical planning involved.

As tempting as it may be, you don’t need to add-to-cart every single item you see on ‘Must Have Disney Essentials’ lists. Before you start shopping, it pays to think through what will help your family enjoy your trip the most. The best travel products for families will vary, so evaluate these factors before you start shopping:.

Sources indicate that of course, start with the makeup of your family. How old will your kids be on the trip, and what needs and preferences correspond with their ages? Strollers are a big decision for many, and there are lots of pros and cons to consider: Will it help or hurt to have a stroller for airports? Is it worth it to lug a stroller to the parks? Would renting Disney World strollers be a better option? The answer will be different for every family, so don’t listen to advice that insists on a right answer. Our youngest was six on our trip and I seriously considered taking or renting a stroller. She ended up walking the parks like a champ and I was glad we didn’t have to deal with a stroller! Had she been a year younger, though, I am sure a stroller would have been our saving grace.

What are your kids most looking forward to in the parks? How will they handle long lines? Will you need to anticipate an afternoon nap each day? Should you stock up on a few fun toys ahead of time so your kiddos aren’t pining for the theme park loot, or do you just need to upgrade your child’s luggage? A Disney World vacation will look very different depending on the ages of your kids, so narrow your list of essentials based on them.

According to recent reports, A surefire way to preemptively ruin your first trip to Disney World is to forget your own needs in the process. For parents, Disney World is fun, sure, but there’s also a lot of planning, incessant crowds, unrelenting heat, not to mention the never-ending soundboard of the kids' needs and wants. Take a moment and think about what essentials you need to make the most of the trip, and perhaps even a few indulgent spa day gifts to help melt stress away at the end of a non-stop Disney World day.

A travel-size umbrella that offers heavy-duty weather protection.

Weather is a major factor in whether Disney World lives up to being “the happiest place on earth.” You likely know to expect warmer temperatures year-round, and extreme heat in the summer. But surprise rain showers are also a common occurrence in Orlando. Luckily, the Repel Compact Umbrella can help on both fronts. Not only will you be happy you have it if you get caught in a shower, but it will also filter UV rays when the sun is beating down. In fact, Repel even offers a UPF 50+ UV protection version of the umbrella to block out 99% of UV rays.

Industry observers note that the umbrella's double-vented canopy is designed to withstand winds up to 85 MPH, so you won’t have to worry about it inverting. It is a heavy-duty umbrella packed into a compact travel size, opens and collapses with a push of a button, and is definitely worth tossing in your park bag. Reviewers say it performs as advertised – one even said the umbrella “loves wind” – with just a few saying the only issue they’ve had is closing it. (And yes, Disney World does allow umbrellas!).

This microfiber towel will save the day in all sorts of ways when you’re out and about, and packs into its own travel bag.

When you’re at the parks from sun up to sun down, unexpected needs are bound to arise, and the Rainleaf Microfiber Towel will be a lifesaver for many of them. Kid drop Dole Whip down their shirt? Want to dry off a wet seat? Need to add more sun shade to the stroller? Chances are you’ll be reaching for this towel all day long. Not only is it compact and made for travel, but it also absorbs five times its own weight and dries incredibly fast. If it’s super hot, drench the towel in cold water to help you cool off, then drape it over your backpack or stroller as you walk around to let it air dry.

Running from $9 to $20 a piece, depending on the size, it’s worth giving each family member their own, or grabbing a few to designate for certain purposes – one for clean up, one for shade and sweat, and one as a picnic blanket for parades or just a quick rest.

This compact travel charger keeps your devices topped up all day long.

According to recent reports, between taking a million pictures and using the Disney app to do everything from making meal orders and reservations to finding the next ride (or nearest restroom!), you’ll be using your phone a lot in the parks. The Anker Portable Charger ensures your devices stay charged up all day long. It has a universal USB-C cable and delivers 10,000mAh (milliamp hours), delivering the equivalent of two full smartphone charges. At 30W charging speed, you can expect it to fully charge a phone in about an hour – which is how long you’ll be lining for some rides anyway.

It has been revealed that the charger is just a tad bigger than a credit card, and weighs about as much as a phone. It can charge three devices at once (you just need extra charging cables) and the cable connector stores in the battery pack for safekeeping between uses. Coming in under $30, it’s well worth the peace of mind so you don’t miss a single picture-perfect moment, even as the last firework illuminates the night sky.

One tip I got from a Disney World cast member is to take screenshots of the QR codes, order confirmations, lightning lane arrival windows, and anything else you may need for reference from the My Disney Experience App so you aren’t constantly having to access the app, which can drain your phone battery.

Take a rest whenever you need to with this super practical compact folding stool.

The Boreeman Folding Stool is as close as it gets to realizing the idea of pants that turn into a chair, but arguably way more practical. If your back just isn’t what it used to be, or you’ve got a kiddo who you know will complain about standing in line, this folding stool will single-handedly save your Disney World trip. The collapsible seat locks into place at various heights up to 17.72 inches. It packs down into a disc that is 9.84 inches by 2.36 inches with a carrying strap for added convenience. Use it in ride lines, waiting for parades or highlights, or just whenever you need to take a load off. It also comes in handy to help little ones with bathroom needs.

The stool is highly rated with 4.4 stars from over 8,000 reviewers, but some say it’s not super comfortable, while others warn theirs broke while sitting on it. Still, other reviewers say they still use theirs often over a year later. It comes in tons of fun colors and can slide into bags, backpacks, or stroller compartments. It’s also light enough at 2.5 pounds for many kids to carry it through a ride line themselves.

Make any moment magical with these Disney-themed bubble wands.

The struggle to not buy every cute thing you see in Disney World is real, and the Little Kids Disney Light and Sound Musical Bubble Wand is here to help. Light-up bubble wands are all the rage in the parks, and they come with a hefty price tag. If you’re looking to save money where you can on your trip, surprise your little one with a pre-bought bubble wand for a fraction of the cost of the park varieties, which cost upwards of $35.

Industry observers note that these wands are themed with all their favorite characters, including Mickey Mouse, Tiana, Elsa, Moana, and more. They light up, play music, and come with extra bubbles so your kiddo can join in the bubble wand fun all day long. Some reviewers were not satisfied with the durability and quality of the wand, while others say it was perfect for their Disney Parks trip.

Outsmart unpredictable weather with this family pack of reusable ponchos.

According to recent reports, my family didn’t end up needing the Lingito Rain Ponchos Family Pack for rain, but we were so glad we used them on Tiana’s Bayou Adventure! We got in one of the first virtual queue time slots of the morning, and without the ponchos, we would have been utterly soaked for the rest of the day. This family pack gets the job done at keeping your family (and your backpacks) dry, whether the water is weather or ride-related. The adult ponchos have drawstrings, and while I understand they might pose a hazard for kids, I wish the kid ponchos could tighten for a better fit. My kids held theirs closed just under their chins when we dropped down the log flume.

According to recent reports, they come compactly packed in small disposable bags, and you’ll be hard-pressed to fold them back in after you open them. The Amazon listing describes these ponchos as both reusable and disposable, which is accurate. While they can be dried out and used again on a trip, they might be too much trouble to save for your next adventure (however, one reviewer reports their family has used their set again and again). Still, at $10 for a pack of four (two adult and two kid-sized ponchos), they are well worth throwing in your bag every day in case you get caught in one of those notorious surprise Orlando rain showers – or just so you stay dry on wet rides.

This wearable fan rests around your neck for hands-free cooling wherever you go.

If you're worried about the relentless Orlando heat more than any other part of your Disney trip, do yourself a favor and pack the FrSara Portable Neck Fan. It’s encased blade vents blow air all the way around the back of the neck and out the ends to keep you noticeably cooler without having to worry about hazards like tangling hair. With a noise level of 25 dB – the equivalent of the ambient noise of a ‘silent’ PC – you can even keep it running indoors through those winding ride lines without being a nuisance to yourself or others …though it’s worth noting that some reviewers find it too loud.

The fan's working time ranges from four to 16 hours, and its USB-C charging port means you can recharge on the go with a portable device charger. With three speeds and 360-degree surround airflow, it might not quite make you forget you’re in Orlando, but it can certainly take the edge off the heat.

This lightweight travel stroller folds down easily and has four recline positions with tons of storage.

Industry observers note that to pack a stroller or not to pack a stroller, that is the question for families making the pilgrimage to Disney World. If you decide to bring your own, the Summer Infant 3Dlite Stroller is our pick for Disney World for a few reasons. First, the stroller complies with Disney World’s list of prohibited items regarding stroller size, and reviewers do confirm that they used this stroller in Disney World. Second, the price is right at under $100, though it’s worth noting that single-stroller rentals at Disney World go for $15 per day, and $13 per day for multi-day rentals.

It has been revealed that the stroller is lightweight, has four recline positions for napping on the go, a pop out weather canopy, and tons of extra storage, including a cup holder, close-top bag, and large storage compartment underneath the seat. Reiewers agree that this is a great, budget-friendly stroller for travel, and is highly rated at 4.6 stars with over 7,000 reviews. Plus, it has a weight capacity of 50 pounds, which is on the upper end for most travel strollers. So if you have an older kid who might not be able to last the entire day on foot, this stroller can be a lifesaver.

Take it from me, even anxious, stressed-out parents can make the most of their family’s first trip to Disney World. Resolve to manage your stress level by taking good care of yourself, setting yourself up for success by planning based on what will make it magical for your family, and packing essentials that will help everyone enjoy the trip.

In a recent development, the key is managing expectations, especially your own. Knowing that a vacation with kids is still parenting, just in a different location – and understanding that parenting in Disney World isn’t always a walk in the park – can help you make this trip every bit as magical for your kiddos as you hoped, though it likely won’t feel like it to you. So make sure you stop and take in their sweet faces when they meet their favorite characters, when they go on the ride they were so excited for, and as they watch as fireworks illuminate the night. You’ll experience the magic, guaranteed!

It has been revealed that want a more decadent drink for a movie marathon at home? You have to try Princess Pinky Girl’s apple cider float recipe. It’s basically like a milkshake and apple cider had a baby and then dressed it up in warm, seasonal spices.

While technically not a mocktail in that it’s not imitating a cocktail, a gussied-up take on hot chocolate still feels really festive and exciting to try.

In a recent development, this apple cider shrub mocktail from Budget Bytes is the drink if you like a not-so-sweet mocktail that tastes almost like it could be boozy. The drink has a few steps that’ll make you look like a professional bartender, but it’s easy enough that even a first-timer around a cocktail shaker can pull it off. Bonus points: They’re also incredibly cheap to make.

Princess Pinky Girl’s recipe will teach you how to get the perfect balance of flavors if it’s your first time wading into dirty soda territory.

  • In a recent development, for those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that american kids are having a mental health crisis like no other. What are we to do with all these diagnoses?

It has been revealed that in a New York Time ideas story that ran this past week, Jia Lynn Yang opens with a bang: “One of the more bewildering aspects of the already high-stress endeavor of 21st-century American parenting is that at some point your child is likely to be identified with a psychiatric diagnosis of one kind or another. Many exist in a gray zone that previous generations of parents never encountered.”.

In a recent development, for those with tweens and teens, this might seem obvious. For those with younger ones, buckle up.

Industry observers note that in Yang’s story, she focuses on the role schools play. Failures in education may lead to an increase of psychiatric diagnoses like ADHD — alongside IEPs or maybe medications — as a means to catch up kids who are being lost in crowded, test-reliant, merit-funded schools. Of course, even Yang points out that schools are only one part of the puzzle. There’s screens and social media taking over our emotional lives and psychiatric development; the pandemic’s long-felt chilling effect on socialization; the adult world of division and anger in politics and everywhere else; and of course changes within the Mental Health Industrial Complex.

It has been revealed that it’s this last piece that Dr. Sami Timimi, a child and adolescent psychiatrist and psychotherapist at the National Health Service in the United Kingdom is focused on. He's the author of six books including Naughty Boys: Anti-Social Behavior, ADHD, and the Role of Culture and his most recent book, Searching for Normal, which promises to outline a new approach to understanding mental health, distress and neurodiversity. There little doubt we could use some advice here — and a bit of demystification around the mental health crises that seems to have taken over childhood.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

I frankly found Searching for Normal to be a difficult book. The science and ideas are very clearly laid out, but you're throwing a lot of stones systemically and culturally that are not often cast. As a layperson and a parent with a house filled with diagnoses, medications, cultural shame, and lots of doubts about our mental health journey, the paralysis you describe feels very close to home. Given all this, I'm wondering, significant picture, what is the main takeaway you'd want a parent to walk away with from your book?

According to recent reports, dr. Sami Timimi: It is a difficult read because we have a public narrative that's been around for a while that's really created a mythology around what we think of in terms of mental health and behavioral difference. My main message is that what we are calling psychiatric diagnosis aren't really diagnoses. And be careful where the culture of diagnoses might lead you to, because we have so much evidence now that the way we're approaching mental health has resulted in something called the treatment prevention paradox, where at a population level we're seeing increasing prevalence of mental conditions and mental health diagnoses. At the same time we're seeing an increasing number of people accessing various types of treatments associated with these diagnoses.

Industry observers note that but we're not seeing an improvement in the outcomes. If we saw an improvement in the outcomes, we would expect at least a stabilization and hopefully a reduction in prevalence of certain conditions because they would be being effectively treated. I don't think there's actually much disagreement with this in most of the academic literature on what's going on because mental health does seem to be an outlier compared to we've seen a lot of progress in physical health.

It has been revealed that for example, when I was a kid, if I got leukemia, my chances of survival into adulthood was around 20%. Now it's around 80%. So this is what happens when you have approaches that are built on technical knowledge that allows you to understand what's going on and make specific treatments for it. But it seems to be the case in mental health that we're going in the wrong direction. What are the assumptions that go missing when we approach mental health as if it's physical health? Because we have to remember, there's no brain scan for ADHD, there's no blood test for anxiety. You can't examine a thought under a microscope. And it becomes difficult to sit in that area of uncertainty and curiosity.

You talk about the TikTok contagion of health disorders and you cite the, I think it was 2023 research about Canadian teen girls presenting with a variety of self-described disorders that are all relatively rare. I'm wondering if you can describe the phenomenon and then I wonder, what does it change for parents on the ground? We have to take their thoughts seriously, no?

In a recent development, yeah, that's a difficult one, isn't it? It's interesting because I heard about this research from a colleague and friend of mine who's a psychiatrist in Canada who shared this paper and it happened just at the point where I was seeing that in my clinical work as well, I was seeing young people who were brought by their parents, parents very worried, with presentations that are generally considered to be quite rare presentations. So, for example, I saw a number of kids who were coming and saying that they had these Tourette's symptoms but they had no history of it. It's like it suddenly emerged.

It is hard because first of all, I don't blame social media for causing these things because actually a lot of this is narratives that's been suggested and started out. The bigger phenomena are these influencers who say that they have ADHD or autism or anxiety and they publicize it online and they talk about things that are signs of potentially having these conditions. And we have to remember, growing up is tough. Try to remember what I was like as a 13, 14-year-old — it is a struggle. There's a lot of changes going on.

You're in a phase of your life where you're seeking meaning and you're seeking belonging and you're involved in those existential type of scenarios where you're trying to figure out where do I fit in? What's my life all about? And so what's been happening is because they watch a lot of these things online with a lot of the influencers just taking up concepts that have been given to them by certain branches of academic psychiatry. And so what social media is doing is a kind of a social contagion. It's turbocharging these ideas and spreading them out.

This goes alongside a trend that's been happening in parenting.

I think a lot of parents have lost their trust that they know what they're doing. I think a lot of parents have lost their confidence. They feel the need to go to see a professional to try and understand. And it's difficult when a lot of the professionals are also involved in what I call the Mental Health Industrial Complex. This is how they get paid, this is how they earn a living.

And so one of the things that I do encourage parents to do is don't be scared of your children. Don't be scared of their intense emotions and don't be scared of conflict. Conflict happens. What has I think happened as we've exported the knowledge base to professionals is we've also developed a curious form of something that some people refer to as cognitive parenting. I know the concept of helicopter parenting, cognitive parenting is a little bit different where you try to reason things through, where you treat your children as if they're already developed adults.

So what role should parents take?

If you don't think this is good for your children, tell them. If you want to put some boundaries around them, don't be afraid of their conflicts.

In a recent development, I liken it a little bit to a referee in, well, for us it's a soccer match. Whenever they, say, blow the whistle that there's a foul committed, the offending team that you've blown the whistle for will complain. That's what happens.

It has been revealed that the crowd will complain as well and say the referee is biased and so on. So when you are a rule enforcer, one way to think about it is you're not going to get any good feedback. You're always going to get protests. You have to ride that out. But a good referee delivers the consequence. The consequence is usually fairly short, it's fairly immediate. Don't delay the consequences because you don't say, well, I've seen you doing that foul, but the next match you have, if you do that again, then the next match you have, I'm going to give this or that. Whatever consequence it is, immediate, short-lived, doesn't have to be long. Just something that shows that you disapprove and this is not allowed.

Industry observers note that and the other thing you do is you don't argue with them. So in soccer matches, you have a half-time where the teams go into the dressing room for 15 minutes before coming. You don't see a referee running after the player who's committed the foul telling them, “I've seen you, I've seen you doing this in other matches. You think you're going to get away with it. You never learn, you never listen.” A good referee spots the infringement, knows that they're going to get back chatted and they're going to get flak, needs to develop a thick skin to ride that out, not rise to it and doesn't get involved in nagging them and so on. And once the consequence is delivered, it's over. Don't need to talk about it again. It's finished.

According to recent reports, what happens when you get caught in what you call the Mental Health Industrial Complex? A quote in the book that really resonated with me, asks “What might happen if instead of shaping the treatment around diagnosis, it was put to one side and the specific challenges, fears, and context were engaged with instead?” Can you answer the question you pose? What does that exactly look like?

Recent findings suggest that so one of the things, understanding that what we call psychiatric diagnoses are not actually diagnoses, they're descriptions. They're what a branch of therapy referred to as narrative therapy ...[which] basically states that our life is made up of stories. It's the stories we hear about ourselves, the stories others tell about us, and we build up a set of stories to understand ourselves. We're surrounded by narratives. And the narratives we tell ourselves have a powerful impact on how we experience our emotions.

In a recent development, so what I was describing there is instead of falling down the root of imagining that if you get a diagnosis you found the meaning for what it is that is going on that's troubling you, there is a different way of trying to find out what it is you're trying to achieve, what is it the difference that you're trying to make, that a diagnosis can't do. So one thing I do in my clinical life is a form of what's referred to as Socratic questioning.

Let's say you got a diagnosis and it was the perfect diagnosis and you felt it fitted. What difference do you imagine this is going to make to your life? What difference is that going to make to your life?

It has been revealed that A diagnosis in a sense is an abstract thing. It doesn't really tell you specifically materially what's going on in your world. Is it that actually you're having trouble with friendships? Is it that your family is under stress and you're under stress because you think your parents are about to split up? Is it that you're finding yourself out of your depth at school? So you're trying to get to the specifics of what it is that people are wanting to see change in their life.

Right. Keep questioning the outcomes and ideas. I really like this tool for parents.

And the other thing is I'm trying to help people move past the idea that experiencing intense emotions is a sign that there's something wrong in them. Experiencing intense emotions is something that we all have to go through. If we don't go through it, we have less of a chance to develop psychologically.

In a sense, the role of parents is to be careful about saving your children from struggle and suffering because that is an unrealistic goal. All life involves struggle and suffering at some level. How can we know joy if we don't know sadness? It's impossible.

It has been revealed that you say this is the most pathologized generation ever. Given that, do you have a checklist for parents to look through and say, is my child being pathologized?

In a recent development, that's an interesting question. I may be averse to the whole concept of checklists, partly because in understanding that all our definitions of mental health are subjective. So our understanding of what is and isn't a kind of looming problem that needs some sort of professional intervention. There is no formula that will allow you to figure this one out. It's going to have to be situation, person and family specific.

One thing I say to parents is, look, all good parents feel guilty. That's just a given. I cannot help you with that. Whatever I do, whatever anybody does, you'll carry on feeling guilty or worry, have I done too much of this? Have I interviewed too little? Have I given too much advice? Have I given the wrong? That's what good parents do. Be careful about that guilt driving you to do too much. And I think that's now a bigger danger than the opposite. So we end up intervening perhaps unnecessarily without holding our own anxiety and our own guilt. So one of my little messages is don't try too hard.

On that note, what do you do with the massive feelings in a household? How do you let issues not get carried away?

Industry observers note that so one of the things that I try to work with with families is understanding, I use the metaphor of a dance, that there's emotional flow going between people and that emotional flow defines how that relationship works. And sometimes what happens is that anger becomes the dominant way in which connection happens.

The other thing I think about in terms of emotions, I think of emotions as being viral. You catch the emotions of the person closest to you. If your kid is angry with you, it's very hard not to get angry back at them. So kind of developing an awareness of that emotional flow of how it's working in your particular relationship and developing an understanding that that has become a dance.

Industry observers note that for example, I know there was a period in my own kid's life where there was a lot of tension, a lot of sibling rivalry to the point where our son and daughter were getting physical and losing temper. And we thought, me and my wife thought only one of them would survive in childhood. That's what it felt like to us.

Anyway, so I thought, okay, well I have to try and do something about this. So I started writing little post-its at the end of each day, just a few, a sentence or two about things that I liked that happened and I just stuck it above their bed before they went to bed.

After a couple of weeks of doing this, my daughter said to me, "Dad, you're being weird." And I said, "What do you mean I'm being weird?".

"Why do you keep putting these post-its and saying these nice things?" I said, "Okay, do you like it?".

So just something also a bit playful a bit, but it's just about trying to refine that emotional connection somewhere other than what's become the defining dance.

A little bit of, “all you need is love.” And I think you had it at the top of one of your chapters, quoting Confucius.

Recent findings suggest that exactly. The journey of a thousand miles starts with the first step.

#79374. Breaking: It's Time to Stop Tracking Screen Time — And Start Living In the Digital Age

📅 02 Dec 2025 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3049 w)
