Latest Update: How To Make Fewer Grocery Trips & Still Eat Well

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1369 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more.
  • It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks.
  • The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Groceries cost a fortune, gas isn’t cheap… every “quick” run to the store somehow costs you 60 bucks or more. Experts share how to shop less and still feed your family well.

It’s a phenomenon that happens more often than not these days: You run into the store for milk, cheese, eggs, and a few other basics, and walk out wondering how in the hell a small handful of grocery bags just set you back upwards of 100 bucks. Worse, you then have to play budget Tetris, moving money around to make sure you have funds for the inevitable grocery run you’ll have to make next week. Add in the gas it takes to get to and from, and you’re spent literally and figuratively.

The reality is groceries are still painfully expensive, and plenty of families are stretched thinner than ever. And, sure, cutting back on trips is probably one of the easiest and most logical ways to save money (and time, and sanity). But it begs the question: How long can you go between grocery runs without your family surviving on cereal benders?

We asked food and budgeting experts how they personally make it work.

Most of the experts we polled said one significant shop a week is sort of the sweet spot. “Every extra trip not only takes up valuable time, but is also another chance to grab things that aren’t on the list and drive up your overall grocery bill,” says Laurie Hise, CEO of Passionate Penny Pincher.

According to recent reports, is it possible to stretch it to every two weeks? Maybe. But AJ Prasaguet, head of the iconic Palace bar and restaurant in Miami Beach, points out that biweekly shopping “can work if you have the storage space, freezer capacity, and money available upfront. Those are real considerations, and not every household has all three.”.

It has been revealed that amber Hanson, a licensed nutritionist and founder of Whole You Nutrition, emphasizes that there’s no cut-and-dry, one-size-fits-all answer. Your ideal grocery-shopping cadence will ultimately depend on things like how close you live to a store and when your paycheck hits the bank. If you get paid every two weeks, it might make sense to shop on that timeframe too.

Before you make your little grocery list and head to the store, open up your own fridge, freezer, and pantry. “The best way to save money is to use what you have already paid for,” claims Hanson.

In a recent development, jenn Lueke, Newly introduced York Times-bestselling author of Don’t Think About Dinner, does her inventory every Friday night, then builds the next week’s meals around what’s left. Example: “If I know I have a half carton of broth that needs to be used, I’ll make sure to pick up a grain, like rice or quinoa, that I can cook in it.”.

Industry observers note that prasaguet goes one step further. “Give an ingredient its next job before you buy it. If a recipe needs half a container of something, decide where the other half is going.” Take cabbage, for instance. It can be slaw one night, stir-fry the next, and soup filler after that.

Another tip Hise is a fan of is ordering online for pickup or delivery when you can. The simple act of skipping the aisles means you don't have to worry about impulse buys wreaking havoc on your total.

In a recent development, as a busy working mom who regularly feels she has to have everything for the week figured out at all times, this was very liberating to hear! As the experts remind us, life happens. Plans change. A rigid seven-night menu is a fast track to wasted food.

Sources indicate that but if it makes you feel better to have the week mostly lined up, you could follow Hise’s example: plan five “fresh” dinners a week, leaving one night for leftovers and one for a meal pulled from what’s already in the pantry, fridge, or freezer. Prasaguet relies on a similar formula: four planned dinners, one leftovers meal, one pantry or freezer dinner, on flex night. “That gives the week some structure without pretending everything will go according to plan,” he says.

Lueke recommends starting with dinners, then exploring how you can make the most of them. “Will the slow-cooker chicken stretch to cover lunches for half the week too? Can I make a double batch of quinoa and bulk up our mid-week sheet pan dinner?” Theme nights like Taco Tuesday or Breakfast for Dinner also help reduce decision fatigue.

The trick to making groceries last, many of the pros explained, is buying foods with different lifespans and eating them in the right order. “You do not want an entire cart of produce that all needs attention at once,” emphasizes Prasaguet.

Lueke thinks about it in three zones:.

Andrea Woroch, a consumer savings expert, notes that some hardy produce (think garlic, potatoes, sweet potatoes, winter squash, even whole apples) can last for months depending on storage conditions as well as how they’re handled. For fast-spoilers like berries, resist the urge to buy the giant fresh packs unless you know your family will gobble them down. Otherwise, stock up on frozen.

If you're afraid frozen and canned food won't pack the same nutritional punch as fresh, well, the experts beg to differ.

Industry observers note that “One of the biggest misconceptions about healthy eating is that fresh foods are always better than frozen or canned alternatives. That’s simply not the case,” claims Jennifer Pallian, a registered dietitian and founder of Foodess. Frozen vegetables are typically flash-frozen shortly after harvest, and research has found they can be just as nutritious as fresh produce that’s been sitting in your fridge for several days. In some cases, they even have more vitamin C.”.

Sources indicate that don’t turn your nose up at canned staples, either. Pallian is a big proponent of canned light tuna (a solid source of protein, selenium, and omega-3s) and canned chickpeas, which pack both protein and fiber and are already cooked.

Just opt for low-sodium or no-salt-added canned veggies and beans, and be mindful of foods packed in juices, syrups, or sauces.

Adopting a few little habits can go a long way toward making food last until your next grocery run:.

However, Prasaguet reminds us, “Stretching groceries should never mean stretching food safety.” That means refrigerating leftovers within two hours, eating them within three to four days, or sticking them in the freezer.

According to recent reports, you should know that eating well doesn’t mean you have to buy a bunch of fancy superfoods. “Some of the most nutrient-dense foods in the grocery store are also the cheapest,” Hanson says.

Here’s what our experts say they keep stocked:.

It has been revealed that and while many of us think shopping in bulk must save money, Prasaguet notes that it’s “only better value if you can afford it, store it, and finish it.” Hise’s workaround is to grab a few extra cans whenever they’re on sale. “A few extra cans a month can add up to a pantry that carries you through a tight month.”.

If you feel like a failure every time you serve your family dinner out of a bag or can, it’s high time you cut yourself some slack.

According to recent reports, “Frozen and canned foods that you actually eat beat fresh vegetables you throw away every time,” notes Hise. Link agrees, adding, “I’d much rather see a family use convenient foods they enjoy than buy fresh ingredients that become a science experiment in the crisper drawer.”.

Recent findings suggest that “A fed family is a win, and ‘fresh’ isn’t the measure of a good dinner," Lueke puts it simply. A balanced meal is made up of a protein, a plant or two, and something filling. It truly does not matter if those came from the produce section or the freezer aisle.

It has been revealed that but maybe Prasaguet sums it up best. “You do not have to prove your love through a complicated dinner,” he reassures. “Feeding your family with the resources you have is already an act of care.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Discover the beauty, meaning, and cultural stories behind 250 captivating Turkish names.

Have you ever met someone and immediately thought, Of course that’s their name?

Maybe their name sounds soft and peaceful, and that is exactly how they carry themselves. Perhaps it feels bold and powerful, matching their confidence before they have even said a word. It can make you wonder how parents choose the perfect name for a baby they have only just met, and how they somehow know which name will grow to suit them.

Choosing a name often means imagining who that baby might become. Parents may be drawn to a particular meaning, family tradition or simply the way a name sounds, hoping it will feel right both in the first moments of life and many years later.

Names become part of how we understand people. Over time, they collect memories, personality traits, family stories and emotions. A name chosen for a newborn may begin with a meaning, a tradition or simply a beautiful sound, but it eventually becomes inseparable from the person carrying it.

It has been revealed that names can carry the same meaning and still sound completely different from one language to another. A name inspired by the moon may feel soft and luminous in one culture, yet bold, mysterious or quietly powerful in another.

Turkish names are especially rich in imagery. Many draw from the sky, the sea, the seasons and the natural world, turning a single word into something vivid and memorable. Aylin evokes a halo around the moon, Deniz and Derya call to mind the sea, Gunes means sun and Yildiz means star.

Others reflect qualities parents may hope their children will carry through life. Eren is associated with wisdom, Mert with bravery and honesty, and Umut with hope.

With roots in Turkic, Arabic, Persian and neighboring traditions, names used in Türkiye reflect a layered cultural history shaped by poetry, nature and generations of meaning.

It has been revealed that below are 100 names commonly used in Türkiye, presented in alphabetical order. The list includes feminine, masculine and gender-neutral options.

Akin – warrior or one who advances.

Alara – water fairy or mythic river spirit.

Arda – successor or one who follows.

Atalay – celebrated or renowned.

Ayaz – frost or cool, clear air.

Aysun – as beautiful as the moon.

Cagdas – contemporary or modern.

Candan – sincerely or from the heart.

Ceyda – graceful or beautiful woman.

Dilara – one who delights the heart.

Ebru – marbled pattern or cloudlike design.

Egemen – sovereign or independent.

Ekim – October or sowing season.

Ekin – harvest or cultivated field.

Elvan – colorful or multicolored.

Emine – trustworthy or faithful.

Emre – friend or loving companion.

Eren – wise or spiritually mature.

Erkan – noble or courageous man.

Esra – swift or nighttime traveler.

Evrim – evolution or transformation.

Gokce – heavenly or sky-colored.

Gurkan – strong or proud lineage.

Kamuran – fortunate or successful.

Koray – glowing or ember-colored moon.

Mine – enamel or delicate ornament.

Oguz – strong or historic Turkic tribe.

Omer – flourishing or long-lived.

Orhan – great ruler or army leader.

Sila – reunion with one’s homeland.

Tarkan – warrior or noble title.

Yaren – close friend or companion.

Zumra – emerald or precious stone.

#79323. How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1034 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scarymommy ↗ Open Full Page

How To Have A Lazy Thanksgiving Without Losing That Holiday Magic

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1034 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scarymommy

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.
  • Recent findings suggest that as a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year.
  • Industry observers note that who decorated the house like that?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Delegate the sides, veto the cranberry sauce, and actually sit down at your own table.

Recent findings suggest that as a child, I remember the holiday season feeling like the most magical time of the year. Thanksgiving, in particular, seemed like a massive deal because it meant Christmas was right around the corner. The house always felt so warm and cozy with fall decorations on full display — their last hurrah before Christmas took over. And the food. There was always so much delicious food to consume. It was wonderful. It was special. And now, as an adult, I realize it was all thanks to... my mom.

Industry observers note that who decorated the house like that? Mom. Who invited the guests and organized the whole Thanksgiving affair? Mom. Who made all of that yummy food? You guessed it — Mom! For me, all of that stuff just seemed to magically get done without much fuss. But there was a fuss. And it wasn’t magic. It was Mom. And now that I’m a mom myself, I realize just how much she had on her plate, figuratively speaking. (Literally, she probably didn’t have much on her plate at all because she was too busy hosting to actually enjoy the meal she created.).

Sources indicate that the point is, Thanksgiving can prove to be such a stressful time for moms with all the planning and cooking and putting everyone else’s needs above their own. So much effort is put into making this day perfect for everyone but themselves. But moms deserve to enjoy this holiday too, which is why I say it’s time to invoke a fresh tradition known as the Lazy Thanksgiving.

Industry observers note that now I know what you’re thinking, but don’t let the name fool you; a Lazy Thanksgiving doesn’t mean a Lame Thanksgiving. There are still plenty of ways to make this day feel special without completely wiping yourself out in the process. Here’s how.

Even if you’re hosting Thanksgiving dinner, that doesn’t mean you should automatically carry the load of the entire meal on your shoulders. Do what any good boss does and delegate an assortment of dishes to other members of the family for them to bring over on the day of. If there’s one thing that you personally enjoy making, then by all means have at it. But everything else should be outsourced to others. Don’t let the burden fall solely on you.

Sources indicate that to add a fun twist, reveal that anyone who contributes a dish gets their name entered into a raffle for a special prize at the end of the night. This could be something hassle-free and small, like a cute little ornament or a goodie bag of chocolate. This not only serves as a great incentive to help lighten your cooking load, but it also gives the winner a sweet keepsake of the occasion. (It’s worth noting that this prize part is completely optional — no family member should need to be bribed to help out.).

Recent findings suggest that if you don’t feel comfortable with a potluck approach, but still feel overwhelmed at the thought of making so many dishes, feel free to just simply not make some of those items. (Think of it as a food-ocracy and you’re the president.) Cranberry sauce may be thought of as a Thanksgiving staple, but if only a spoonful or so gets eaten each year, then you are well within your rights to take it off the menu. The same goes for squash or yams or anything else that never ends up feeling worth the effort you put into making it. Odds are, no one is going to care or miss it, and those who do obtain the right to make it themselves.

If you really want to unburden yourself and maximize your relaxation time, you could always get the food from somewhere else and either pick it up or have it delivered right to your door. Honey Baked is always a solid option with great choices for a delicious holiday feast.

It’s more expensive than making it yourself, but a lot less time-consuming, and if various family members chip in to make it happen, it could end up being more than worth the cost. That way you can sit down and actually have time to enjoy everyone’s company for a change.

Recent findings suggest that do you enjoy cooking but dread the massive clean-up job that comes at the end of it all? Trade in regular dishes and cups for paper ones. Sure, there will still be some dishes to contend with that the actual food was cooked in, but this swap definitely helps cut down on the task and leaves extra room for everything else to go in the dishwasher.

As a bonus, you can make use of all the extra paper plates by turning it into a fun craft competition for the kids. Whether they use them to make a snowman or some Thanksgiving-inspired creation, this is a great way to get their artistic juices flowing. Choose a family member to be the judge and give out a prize to the winner each year: something like a small toy or maybe even a NeeDoh if you really want the crowd to go wild and can get your hands on one. The kids will love the challenge and look forward to it as part of an annual tradition.

Industry observers note that then again, do you want to go completely rogue? Throw tradition out the window and order takeout or make an easy casserole that will feed everyone and involve zero stress. No turkey. No stuffing. No gravy. No hassle.

Recent findings suggest that however you choose to invoke your “Lazy Thanksgiving,” just make sure that it’s the right fit for you. The whole point is to put less pressure on this day, and by extension, yourself. Remember that less work for you doesn’t equate to a less enjoyable time for everyone else. You being around more, instead of running back and forth to the kitchen, is something the whole family will be thankful for in the long run.

#79322. Tech Report: I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1200 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Mother ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: I had an equal partnership – and I still became the default parent

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1200 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and unveils he’s going out for something spontaneous.
  • And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.
  • In a recent development, standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, every now and then, my husband picks up his phone and car keys, and unveils he’s going out for something spontaneous. Lunch with a friend. A bike ride. He’s gone in about ninety seconds if I don’t stop him at the door.

And I generally don’t, because I want my husband to have time for himself.

But I also want the same for myself.

In a recent development, standing behind the closed door, I ask: When was the last time I left this house by myself, without planning it, negotiating it, or trading for it? Not once since my first child was born… three and a half years ago. Then it hits me: I am the proverbial default parent.

In a recent development, in my life, I have moved countries on 48 hours’ notice. I have started businesses and communities on four continents, landed in cities where I knew no one, and figured it out from the ground. Yet here I am, unable to walk out my own front door without a negotiation.

Now I am the kind of person who books a haircut six weeks out.

My husband carries himself with the lightness of someone who isn’t carrying the majority of the parenting load.

The mental one: how many diapers, ounces of milk, and clothing changes need to be packed for a single outing. The emotional one: forecasting ways to address my little one’s growing feelings or managing the conditions to prevent a meltdown. The logistical one: managing energy levels and knowing a missed nap isn’t worth the spontaneity of welcoming last-minute visitors (the hosting of which, by the way, would fall on me).

He doesn’t carry any of that because I do. And I know I’m not alone in this. (There are even several Bluey episodes about it).

But I thought my husband and I would be different. And to his credit, he does a lot for the family, and has always been willing to work towards a situation where I felt supported. Still, for over three years, our day-to-day behaviors set our sails in a different direction; the mere idea that we were working toward a mostly equitable deal blinded me to the fact that, too stereotypically, I was the one carrying the invisible load of parenting.

For a while, I stewed silently, filing away every every “just tell me what to do” and every unplanned walk out the door.

But my resentment wasn’t getting me closer to the future I actually wanted, which is to raise my kids alongside a partner I trust. Anger is honest information, but a terrible operating system. It costs you the very thing you’re angry about losing: your own energy.

So I stopped waiting for space to appear and started claiming it. Here are the steps I took:.

The first step was recognizing there was a real problem. Only then could I have a productive, fact-based conversation with my husband.

Sources indicate that what helped: talking it out, sharing the situation with friends and watching them nod before I finished the sentence. Those conversations helped clear the fog and made it clear: I had become the default parent without ever applying for the role, and I needed it recognized as a real job, with real requirements, not something invisible and easily taken for granted.

Sources indicate that clarity is a prerequisite for being heard, and it is what moved the conversations with my husband past defensiveness. Until then, the idea that we had a “mostly equitable deal” was blurring his perspective too.

According to recent reports, we didn’t get it right at once. Several conversations left one of us hurt, misunderstood, or underappreciated. But we persisted in having the difficult ones. Those conversations eventually gave us enough clarity to lay out, with clinical precision, the ways our partnership had been uneven. We could dissect a messy situation and turn resentment into discernment, naming the areas where I was lacking support and the areas where both of us were lacking appreciation.

Clarity let us stand across from each other, our vision for an equitable partnership leading the way instead of resentment for how it had been.

And we learned something more key: an equitable relationship isn’t found. It’s built. That shared understanding made the next steps possible.

Once we both understood what my resentment had been trying to say, in more positive, proactive terms, my needs became clearer and easier to ask for. And my husband finally had something concrete to act on.

We put our partnership to work: I defined clear steps to reclaim my own freedom, and he redefined what it means to be a supportive partner.

From there, we made a real proposal: a family calendar that protects my time the same way it protects his and provides a predictable rhythm. The gym, daily. Tango on Monday nights. A weekday or two blocked out because I’m in the city for meetings. An evening for dinner with a friend.

And, every so often, a half-day on the weekend for my own creative retreat, which is where I am as I type this: in a literal room of my own, my office and studio, with a door that closes.

I still won’t leave the house on a whim. But neither will he. We plan ahead, tell the other person, and arrange childcare if we both want some time out.

Relationships tarnish under unmanaged resentment. Bringing back the shine takes work.

Sources indicate that from my end, I had to listen more, or proactively ask for his perspective on an issue I’d raised, and work to transmute resentment into something more productive: naming my unmet need. I had to really care about his perspective, and trust that he had been going for “supportive partner” all along, even if our early attempts had been clumsy and left scars.

From his end, he needed to become more observant and make efforts to show up more often in ways that were meaningful to me: offering to hire help for things previously expected to come from me, checking in before making plans on his own, and looping me in before inviting friends and family.

In a recent development, we also started scheduling more romance, whether a babysitter-powered date or quality time at home. But I’d say this came as a consequence of everything above: there was no mood for a date while our relationship was permeated by resentment. The difficult conversations had to come first.

Recent findings suggest that the work most mothers do is largely invisible. But invisible isn’t the same as involuntary.

I can’t undo how the default got set, or how my own behavior kept reinforcing it. What I can do is refuse to let the default compromise my own health, my relationship, and the example I’m setting for my children. I want them to have the courage to create a life they’re proud to call theirs.

Some of that courage looks like walking out your own front door on a Saturday, keys in hand, for no reason at all: knowing the little ones are safe, and well cared for, because you made it so.

#79317. Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

📅 27 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1327 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fatherly ↗ Open Full Page

Jefferson Fisher Has The Secret to Getting Along Better With Absolutely Everyone

📅 27 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less.
  • If being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything.
  • For once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the lawyer, author, and influencer wants us to talk more and argue less. He might just be onto something.

If being a parent, a husband, a man, a human has taught me anything at all it’s that communication is everything. Also, most of us suck at communication.

For once, our poor communication is not a product of big external forces — neither isolationist politics nor overcooked capitalism nor a failing of modern masculinity. We can only blame ourselves because, hey, communicating is hard. Getting your point across to a group, your nuclear family, or one single person takes practice and discipline, mistakes and learning. I don’t think we ever get it entirely right.

Well, most of us don’t. There are some communicators in this world that are … blessed. Jefferson Fisher is one such individual. Fisher is a Texan, dad, husband, and personal injury attorney who has made a name for himself through social videos that teach us all how to communicate better.

According to recent reports, the videos offer pithy lessons like this: Instead of saying I disagree, “tweak it a little and say, I see things differently.” Why? “When you talk in terms of perspective, you find more connection.” Here’s another: “How I talk to my kids will affect how they talk to their kids.”.

Sources indicate that simple, pointed, and poignant. You can see why millions tune in.

Fisher’s goal is to make people talk more and argue less. It states just that on the cover of his fantastic, practical, wonderfully written book The Next Conversation — a must read for all of us who strive to get along a little better with those around us.

Recent findings suggest that we caught up with Fisher to talk about his new book and, naturally, anoint him as the latest Cool Dad. Here are some excerpts from our talk, including extras from the Cool Dad Questionnaire and his advice for the most crucial conversations you’ll ever have.

What’s one thing you wish your kids had today from your childhood?

Probably more of a reckless abandon about what they ate. I grew up in just every Little Debbie from Cosmic Brownies to ... everything you could think of that was probably terrible for us, but we didn't know any different.

What does your partner love about you?

In a recent development, I mean, this is my guess ... I would say what Sierra loves about me is my steadiness. When things don't go to plan, I'm pretty rock steady. So when there is something unexpected or the kids go into what we call their midnight madness, when it's right there at bedtime and they're absolutely losing their minds, that's when I'm able to step in and I think I'm able to really notice when she's overwhelmed, and take over.

And what do you think they maybe find annoying about you?

I mean, there's lots. I'm trying to find a really good one like she finds the most annoying about me is sometimes I can be a little bit occasionally of like a party-pooper where the kids are just ... all going nuts and I'm like, "Can we just not yell so much in our house?" So there's that.

Probably the bigger thing she gets more annoyed about is my relationship with money. Its just money. So I'm the spender and so she is the saver. If it's something that's like, "Hey, but this would be fun, even though it's not something we exactly need right now, but it would be a cool memory," I think there's a lot of that.

What does fatherhood mean to you in our current world?

Fatherhood, with the caveat of doing it well to be a good father, I think, is knowing it's a discipline and not a destination. It's a daily devotion to putting your wife, your spouse, your partner, your kids before you. And it's this idea of ... are you inconveniencing them for your comfort or is it the opposite, are you willing to inconvenience yourself for their comfort?

There are times where it's going to be uncomfortable. I don't want to be the one carrying all the bags all the time, but is it what my family needs in that moment in the airport? Yeah, that's what they need. Can I do it? Yeah.

I got to say that the carrying bags all the time is a wonderful metaphor.

Yeah. You're the one that is supposed to shoulder the heavy. So you're supposed to carry what they can't. I'm sure there's a similarity to this phrase of to be what others cannot, you must be willing to suffer what others will not, and so it's like that. To be the dad that others can't, you got to be able to do what others won't.

It has been revealed that how do you better communicate with your partner in parenting? Do you think there's ways that you, something that don't apply, or do you follow the advice in your book and have great arguments and conversations with your spouse?

Industry observers note that I wouldn't say there are things that don't apply. I would say what it would need to go deeper on is the theme of repair specifically. So you could have the mindset of arguments and that's something that's very helpful. There's the idea of saying things with control, meaning be regulated and knowing when you need to take that timeout, and using the pauses. But the turn the book doesn't make with regard to marital relationships is repair.

We are talking about words of affirmation, affirming somebody's feelings, being able to take ownership of your words and what that actually sounds like ... how to truly use words of empathy and affirm how they feel, how to say things that are going to bring. We hit on connection in the book, but more in the way of framing non-relationship conversations.

Industry observers note that in repair, there is a lot of something as simple as, "Yes, I said that. Yes, I did that. I absolutely can see how that would have frustrated you or upset you," or "I think it's totally reasonable for you to feel this way. I don't blame you for being upset about that. I could have done that better." And then how to actually, words of apology, how to repair after a rupture, that to me is, that's a whole different ballgame, whole different set of skills.

It has been revealed that what do you think about checking in? I'm wondering where that falls in the communication line. It's maybe a little bit of the repair, but is that an notable thing to do or how do you feel about just what a felt of unspoken understanding between family?

According to recent reports, there's an element that my wife and I do and that's check-ins and check-outs. I mean, it's what we call them, things that we do in the morning and things that we do in the evening. Otherwise, there are times you may never talk to your spouse in the day and you know what that's like. Before you know it, you're just two people, somehow there's a woman who lives with me. I don't know who she is, but she's here and you can be roommates that way if you're not checking in with each other. The other is that unspokenness of knowing when something is wrong and that you feel like you might be approaching things from a different vantage. I like asking the phrase, "What's coming up?" "What's coming up for you?".

Instead of me saying, "What's wrong with you" or even, "What's up with you?" That tends to get a pretty defensive response. But if I say something as simple as what's coming up, there's a difference between [that and] saying, "How are you and how's your heart?".

#79316. 22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

22 dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy off the shelf

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mother

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.
  • Industry observers note that labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something.
  • Robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a fresh product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Packing a lunchbox snack shouldn’t require a degree, but the snack aisle makes a decent case otherwise.

Industry observers note that labels promise real fruit, no artificial anything and a good source of something. The truth is, most of it is noise. The part that matters is on the nutrition label. For a run of dietitian-approved lunchbox snacks you can buy and pack as-is, we asked two registered dietitians who shop that aisle for a living what they actually look for.

Robin Barrie Kaiden, MS, RD, CDN, CSSD and Lauren Manaker, MS, RDN, LD, both do the same thing with a fresh product before it goes in the cart: They turn it over and read. Here’s what they’re looking for, and the snacks they reach for without overthinking it.

Kaiden scans the label’s ingredients first. “That matters to me more than anything else,” she says. She wants simple, real-food ingredients and the least processed option available. There’s a practical reason to start there, notes Manaker. Ingredients appear in order by weight, so the first few make up most of the product.

Sources indicate that the claims on the front get much less of their attention. “Made with real fruit” doesn’t tell you how much fruit is actually in there, says Kaiden, and “no artificial flavors” doesn’t automatically make something a nourishing snack. Even the regulated claims are narrower than they sound, explains Manaker. “Good source of fiber” means the product provides 10 to 19% of the daily value per serving. “Gluten free” matters for kids with celiac disease or a gluten sensitivity and does nothing nutritionally for anyone else.

The label lists added sugars and total sugars separately. Total sugars include the naturally occurring sugars in ingredients like fruit and milk, states Manaker. Added sugars are the ones put in during processing, and those are the numbers to take into consideration. The targets for added sugar are lower than most parents expect. The Dietary Guidelines for Americans recommend no added sugars for children under 10, and the American Academy of Pediatrics advises less than 25 grams, about 6 teaspoons, per day for kids 2 and older.

According to recent reports, kaiden also looks at where the sugar comes from. She passes on high-fructose corn syrup and would rather see a small amount of honey, maple syrup or coconut sugar. “Those are still added sugars, so the amount matters, but the source and processing matter to me, too,” she says. If cane sugar is on the list, she prefers it farther down.

Industry observers note that protein and fiber make a significant difference in how satisfying a snack is. Kaiden balances a carbohydrate-rich food with protein and some healthy fat, like fruit with nuts, cheese or plain yogurt. “That combination helps slow digestion and supports steadier energy through the afternoon,” she says. For a substantial afternoon snack, she suggests around 5 to 10 grams of protein and at least 3 grams of fiber, depending on a child’s age, appetite and activity level. Those numbers can come from the snack as a whole. No single bar has to do everything.

Sources indicate that most U.S. children don’t get the recommended amount of fiber, says Manaker, so small additions help. Fruit, veggies, beans, whole-grain bread or crackers, and nuts or seeds where school rules allow are all easy lunchbox sources.

It has been revealed that hydrogenated and partially hydrogenated oils are an automatic no for Kaiden. Partially hydrogenated oils contain industrial trans fats, which are particularly harmful to heart health. High-fructose corn syrup, a highly processed sweetener that adds sugar without meaningful nutrition, is another pass.

Seed oils get a lot of negative press, but Kaiden’s position helps clear up confusion: When there’s a comparable option, she opts for extra virgin olive oil or avocado oil instead of seed oils because of the difference in processing. Many seed oils are extensively refined, and some are extracted using solvents such as hexane. “That processing is why I personally prefer other options,” she notes, “not because all seed oils are harmful or because using hexane means unsafe amounts remain in the food.”.

Sources indicate that she’s also not rigid about it. Some Simple Mills crackers contain sunflower oil, and she still buys them for the almond-flour base. “I look at the whole product rather than letting one ingredient make the decision for me,” she says.

Unfamiliar names aren’t automatically a problem, either. Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. Tocopherols are forms of vitamin E that can help preserve freshness. “I care more about what an ingredient actually is than whether its name is easy to pronounce,” indicates Kaiden.

Read the ingredients even on brands you buy regularly, Kaiden cautions, because formulations change, and one good product doesn’t mean everything from that brand makes the cut.

Sources indicate that to make shopping easier for you, we asked the nutritionists exactly what they’re tossing in their carts. Take notes!

According to recent reports, kaiden’s favorite snack doesn’t sound like a dietitian’s pick at all. “Potato chips!” she notes, naming José Andrés Extra Virgin Olive Oil Potato Chips, made with potatoes, extra virgin olive oil and salt. “I want my kids to enjoy their food, and a simple-ingredient chip can absolutely fit into a balanced lunchbox. Add a sandwich and some fruit or vegetables, and you have a lunch that’s nourishing and enjoyable.” Potato chips? Say less.

Tech Report: 18 Easy Bean Recipes For Dinner That Are Cheap & Nutritious

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...).
  • Stuffed peppers are such a flavorful dish that even if you’re a meat-eater, you’ll never miss it in this recipe from All The Healthy Things.
  • Burrito bowls are easy, and they never disappoint.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For a couple bucks a bag? You can’t beat ‘em.

Like most American families, we’ve had to get pretty strategic about our grocery budget over the past year as grocery prices have risen (and risen, and risen...). Since when did a pound of 80/20 become a special little treat? We’ve been opting for ground chicken and ground turkey instead for a few years now. As grocery prices continue to go up, what are you turning to to keep your own food bills down? Maybe it’s rice or lentils, but don’t forget about the humble bean. Canned beans and especially dried bagged beans are affordable sources of protein and fiber, and with the right bean recipes for dinner, you can make them so incredibly delicious. Here’s how to load them up with flavor.

Stuffed peppers are such a flavorful dish that even if you’re a meat-eater, you’ll never miss it in this recipe from All The Healthy Things. Don’t be intimidated by the long ingredient list — most of them are just seasonings you most likely have in your pantry already. These only take about 15 minutes of prep, then just pop them in the oven and go help with homework or baths ‘til they’re done.

Burrito bowls are easy, and they never disappoint. Princess Pinky Girls’ recipe clearly includes chicken, but honestly, if you sub in some really tasty refried beans or something, you won’t even miss it. We are big on burrito bowls in my house because they’re also great work lunches to prep ahead of time.

According to recent reports, chickpeas, aka garbanzo beans, are the filling base to this super flavorful Italian chickpea salad from Foodie Crush. With all the additions — red onion, bell pepper, garlic, pepperoncini, and more — this is a delicious dense bean salad that’ll just get better as the flavors meld together in the fridge all week long.

Averie Cooks’ Mediterranean white bean salad looks exactly like what I mean when I say I want a little snack, but can’t find anything I actually want in the fridge (it’s because I’m looking for a restaurant-quality appetizer at all times). This recipe is a bit more involved, but the marinated white beans, crispy asparagus, and shallots served over whipped ricotta sound good enough to be worth the trouble.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re trying to up your fiber intake, Damn Delicious’ spinach and white bean soup is the recipe for you. This delicious dish is ready in 30 minutes and would be so, so good with some Parmesan grated on top and a side of crusty bread.

In a recent development, chili is a major crowd-pleaser, and it’s a cheap way to make a lot of food at once, especially if you’re subbing in beans for beef. All The Healthy Things’ recipe includes meat, but you can just leave it out. That said, don’t skip the little dash of cocoa powder — it’s a game-changer.

Sources indicate that being able to make some simple but delicious bean sides yourself is a great way to save money, and fortunately, Simply LaKita’s Southern baked beans fit the bill. It takes about an hour, but you’ll have a big batch to pair with other proteins throughout the week.

I’m not sure falafel can be improved upon, but it’s fun to find out. What Jew Wanna Eat’s black bean falafel can be ready in about 20 minutes and doesn’t require many ingredients to pull off. Topped with tomatoes, cucumbers, and tzatziki, this is an easy and filling meal you’ll return to again and again.

Industry observers note that if you’re having a bummer of a week, a cheesy, saucy enchilada night is guaranteed to make you feel at least 1% better. This version from Averie Cooks is a fantastic way to get more veggies into you and your kids, because the sweet potatoes and corn inside will indeed be coated in cheesy deliciousness.

Industry observers note that need a light, yummy salad to eat with chips for lunch? Or something easy to throw into burrito bowls or wraps? All The Healthy Things’ black bean and corn salad is easy to customize with your favorite veggies and herbs, and you can eat it in so many ways.

Filling, cheap taco ideas, you say? Damn Delicious has you covered with these black bean and quinoa tacos. They’re simple, satisfying, and inexpensive — the kind of recipe I could see going platinum in my house, personally.

According to recent reports, foodie Crush’s cannellini beans are another flavorful side you can pair with salads, proteins, or put on toast if you’re into that sort of thing. Or if you’re a fan of brothy beans, you can just grab the pot and a significant spoon and dive in.

In a recent development, princess Pinky Girl is the best at quick, easy recipes that are a breeze to make and super satisfying to eat. This cowboy casserole is also a one-pan meal (love) — it’s sort of like a chili base topped with cornbread. While her recipe calls for ground beef, you could easily just sub in extra beans and veggies.

Sources indicate that haute & Healthy Living’s Italian soup is rich and creamy thanks to a little coconut milk, and incredibly rich in flavor (shout-out to sun-dried tomatoes). The whole thing takes about 15 minutes of prep, and then the slow cooker will handle the rest for you.

Sources indicate that these black bean burgers from Barefoot in the Pines take 35 minutes start to finish (hello, weeknight dinner MVP) and only take two cans of black beans, an onion, and some seasonings to pull off. You can top them with classic burger fixings or go with salsa and guac, as pictured here.

Fried plantains make a regular bowl of beans and rice feel special all of a sudden. This bowl by Cadry’s Kitchen is an easy, affordable meal that gets you all your food groups in one sitting. Like, if you had a nutritionist, they’d be so proud of you.

I love a side of restaurant-style refried beans, but I never think to make them at home. Haute & Healthy Living’s version will help you keep the sodium in check without sacrificing flavor. Eat these as a side, a dip, or load up some bean and cheese burritos.

Beans and rice is a complete meal, and a delicious one at that. This recipe from Biscuits & Burlap is a copycat of Popeye’s red beans and rice side, which, if you’re from the South, you know they’ve got some of the best around.

Which bean dishes will you fall back on to save a few bucks each week?

Max Greenfield Is That Dad

📅 14 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1660 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fatherly

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a new film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.
  • The first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect.
  • Recent findings suggest that greenfield says that understanding the character was easy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a new film, the New Girl star plays a very good dad, naturally.

The first thing you may observe about the dad in Netflix’s upcoming teen drama Don’t Say Good Luck is that his hair looks perfect. That’s only the start of the aspirational cues coming from this character played by Max Greenfield. In this funny — and, yes, tear-jerking — family drama, Greenfield’s character juggles work, elementary-aged twins, a big-feeling teen, and his wife’s cancer diagnosis. While he is at times off-kilter from all that life throws his way in the film, this dad does not bumble his way through it. In every scene, he finds ways to be the emotionally available parent and partner.

Recent findings suggest that greenfield says that understanding the character was easy. “There’s so much of me that’s in that movie,” he tells Fatherly. “I felt so close to what we were doing.” It could be, perhaps, because his daughter, like the main character, is a high schooler; she has mutual friends to the lead actress, Sunny Sandler; and her experience — at least onstage, navigating high school life — just resonated.

We sat down to give Max Greenfield the Cool Dad questionnaire, and then talked about the movie, finding patience, and fighting parental anxiety — and why LA’s bagels are seriously underrated.

This interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sources indicate that I finished watching Don’t Say Good Luck today. I definitely did some crying.

They keep playing clips in these interviews that I’m doing for press, and they’ll play it before the interview, and I’m constantly like, “I need a minute.”.

It’s intense. It’s a wonderful film. I’m wondering how close of a dad are you to who you play on screen in Don’t Say Good Luck. Are you that dad?

Recent findings suggest that I mean, there’s so much of me that’s in that movie. I felt so close to what we were doing. It was really the reason I wanted to do it. My daughter, I think, is a year younger than Sunny [Sandler, the lead], and I was really aware that this was going to be a movie that Sunny was starring in. And from everything that I had heard, I had never done a Sandler movie before, but his sets are famously the best. And so I really wanted to just make sure that she had a comparable experience on this with somebody else. I felt like I knew how to do that.

According to recent reports, my daughter and her have mutual friends, I know where she goes to school… just a lot of the stuff I just was like, “I know this world well.” And so talking to somebody like Sunny is not an problem for me. And trying to be light and supportive in this environment, it was something I felt like I was capable of doing. I didn’t know if I was going to be very good in the movie as an actor, but I was like, “I think I know how to be the dad.” And then there’s the two young boys in the movie, the twins, and they were so funny because they were just never acting. They just were running around.

Recent findings suggest that they’re a little bit younger than my son, but I just coached my son’s basketball team, and wrangling all those kids and getting them going, getting them involved, it was very good prep work for dealing with these two boys. And it made the scenes and made the movie so much fun.

According to recent reports, yeah. Everything was just like, “Oh, this is what my real life is.” And being there with Sunny, I understood that relationship. Being there with the boys, I was like, “I get this relationship.”.

There was a more dramatically real scene later in the movie … I personally had a similar experience to the lead character. My mom had cancer when I was a sophomore in high school, and all I could think about was how I wanted you — your character — to be my dad for that time. For example, that scene when you were sitting in the car and Sunny asked, “Are you okay?” And you asked, “Are you okay?” And both of you noted, “No.” It was just… right.

Sources indicate that that was a really cool scene. Julia Hart, who had directed the movie and wrote the movie along with Laura Hankin and Jordan Horowitz … [had] a lot of conversations about that scene, and they were so generous in my input. It really felt like that scene was going to be the scene for this relationship. And as we started to see how the movie was playing out and what was happening before then, we had sent a bunch of drafts of that scene back and forth to one another, and we all collectively landed in that spot because it really needed to set up everything that comes after that, but it needed to honor everything that was built up before it, and it needed to feel real.

I didn’t want there to be an answer or a fix to what was happening, but I wanted them to feel it, both characters. When we shot that scene, it was nuts. It was really heavy, man.

In this movie, you run a bagel shop. So what’s your order?

Recent findings suggest that oh, wow. Great question. I’ve probably gotten older and more healthy than I need to be, more LA than I need to be. I’ll give you two. One’s an everything bagel [with] just cream cheese, onion, tomato, lox.

It has been revealed that that can’t ever miss, it’s the best. The other one is … either a light cream cheese spread [or] the right type of hummus and then just veggies. But fresh, good veggies that are with the right type of dressing on it and salt and pepper. There’s a place in LA that has been hyped and hyped and I finally went there, I don’t know, a month or two ago. It’s called Courage Bagels. And the line is a mile long. And I was like, “I’m not waiting in line.” And then my daughter and I were like, “Let’s go wait in line.” So we went over there and they had one, I think it’s called the Garden or something. I don’t know. Holy sh*t. It was unbelievable.

One of the big themes of the movie I wanted to get your take on is disclosure to children. That is, what you tell a kid, what you don’t tell a kid, when you’re protecting them from the truth, and when that backfires. I was just wondering if you had thoughts on how you strike that personally.

It’s a really good question. I actually feel like I’ve done a good job with this, personally. There are certain things that I want them to discover on their own, and hopefully my job is to have created a space where they feel comfortable to then bring those things up to me. And then depending on how the question’s asked or how much they want to know, you ease them into certain topics of discussion and what you choose to discover based on what they’re asking. And you let that conversation be ongoing. And so I’ve had some real good success in some areas where those conversations have opened up and become more in-depth over time. And as a result, I see that my kids are way more comfortable with information that I was worried might be confusing or scary. And because they’ve sort of been able to take it in at their pace.

How has your outlook changed now that you’re past the baby and elementary parenting and you have a 16- and 11-year-old?

I’m making a lot more mistakes. That thing we talked about, responsibility versus what to let go, that line is thinner and thinner every day. And there’s so many times where, what are the things that I feel like I need to control to make me feel safer in this situation that is so scary? And being a fear-based parent is not a good zone to operate from.

Sources indicate that and so it’s like my daughter’s now driving and she gets her driver’s license and it’s just like, my wife and I are both like, “Well, so the next day, is she just driving to volleyball practice? Is that how that works?” And if you strip all the fear away from it, you’re like, “Yeah, she practiced and worked up to it and has now passed the test and she’s allowed to legally drive. So yes, why wouldn’t she be able to?” There’s a period of time when they’re small where you’re like, “Yeah, this is just going to keep getting better.” And then it shifts in the most terrifying way and you’re like, “Oh, this is all so much worse.”.

In a recent development, when we were [learning to drive], I would sit in the car with her, we would drive, and I would go, “Oh, you know what? All the anxiety and fear I have about the future and life and work and all the nonsense, that’s not real.” When I’m sitting in a car with my daughter and she’s driving, this is real fear. This is what real fear feels like. It’s like, this is the shark in the water kind of fear. And it’s heavy and it’s tangible. And you almost hold it and you go, “This is what real fear feels like, and this is appropriate for the situation.” So outside of that, when I do feel any sort of anxiety about the future or whatever it is, I go, “Oh, this is not real.” And now I know the difference. So at least I have that.

Hope, grief, happiness, burnout — this week’s confessions have it all.

Is that... dare we say it... hope in the air?! This week’s anonymous mom confessions came in like a tidal wave. Literally, we’ve never seen so many 🌊 emojis in our inbox. Because, yes, moms wanted to talk about the midterms. Hundreds of them! Hope, relief, crying in the kitchen, feeling like they can breathe for the first time in years... along with a few who weren’t celebrating at all. We couldn’t even print a fraction of it, so please know, if you submitted one, you were in extremely plentiful firm.

But what also really struck us was the sentiment underneath: So many moms feel like they’re living in the in-between.

In a recent development, that tracks for the midterm results, obviously. Will we actually see change once the newly introduced class gets sworn in this January? Meanwhile, families are still struggling with inflation and high gas prices and just generally being tired of being broke. This sentiment also surfaced in confessions from moms at crossroads in their relationships, whether it’s the precipice of divorce or considering starting a spicy affair. Moms are feeling it across the board, really, from parenting (the tween years are hitting some of you hard) to health (perimenopause purgatory strikes again).

One mom kind of hit the nail on the head: Her personal life and finances are pretty much in shambles, and also, for the first time in a long time, she feels joy. Both. At once. That’s where a lot of you seem to be right now.

So there’s hope, and there’s the other thing, and most weeks they’re just two wings on the same bird. If that sounds familiar, you’ll likely find a lot of validation in this week’s roundup.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide.
  • Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list says about how we’re shopping this year.
  • Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, each November, Google gives us a peek behind the curtain, synthesising billions of shopping-related searches into their Holiday 100 Gift Guide. The list is built from a full year of Search trends across every category from tech to style. And this year, the toys and games section looks suspiciously like the inside of an elder millennial’s childhood toy chest.

Here are the trending toys parents will want to know about, plus what the list says about how we’re shopping this year.

Searches for “classic toy train set” climbed 240% this year, one of the biggest jumps Google shared. Wooden trains survive toddler teeth, being thrown down the stairs and never fail to get passed down more than once. (Expect the figure-eight to claim your living room floor for the next few years.).

“A ton of play,” Google wrote, and we respect the pun. Searches for stuffed elephant plushies rose 240%, with the Pets Alive Baby Elephant Surprise as the featured pick. Plush is a good pick for a 1-year-old and a 10-year-old alike, and the right one becomes a friend for life.

Searches for the Fujifilm instax holiday set jumped 190%. For tweens, a camera that spits out a real photo is a nice break from the phone, and the prints end up taped to bedroom walls instead of buried in a camera roll. They’ll fly through the film, so tuck a couple of extra packs in the box.

Sources indicate that searches for the FAO Schwarz Piano Mat “struck a chord,” rising 180% in 2026. Anyone who watched Tom Hanks stomp out a duet on the giant keyboard in “Substantial” wanted one of these, and the floor-sized version now fits in a playroom. It’s a sneaky music-and-movement toy for preschoolers. It’s also loud, so choose its permanent residence carefully.

Recent findings suggest that searches for “adjustable roller skates” cruised up 180%. Adjustable skates expand across several sizes, so they can outlast a growth spurt or two. Just remember to add a helmet and pads to the cart.

According to recent reports, some of this may come down to who’s doing the shopping. Millennials make up a massive share of today’s parents, and plenty of us spent our childhoods at the roller rink, building wooden train tracks across the living room rug and waiting for Polaroids to develop. (By impatiently wagging them back and forth, of course.) It’s not hard to imagine a few of these searches coming from parents trying to hand down something that felt magic to them. The best part? There’s a good chance they’ll all still be in rotation when next year’s list comes out.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nick Viall on love, life, and being a twin dad.

In a recent development, nick Viall first appeared on “The Bachelorette” 12 years ago and ever since, he’s had one serious reality TV run. From “Bachelor in Paradise” to “Dancing With the Stars,” “The Masked Singer” to “Age of Attraction,” which he at the moment co-hosts with his wife, Natalie Joy Viall , his handsome mug is everywhere. He also notably doles out relationship advice, also alongside his wife, on the The Viall Files, one of the most popular relationship podcast on Apple that airs three to four times a week.

Sources indicate that what viewers might not know is that this Wisconsinite, the second oldest of 11 siblings, has a two-year-old and, since July, twin infants. So how’s twin dad life? “When you tell people you're expecting ... people are more prone to just kind of, I call doomsday kind of advice,” he tells Fatherly. “And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing.” We caught up to give Nick the Cool Dad questionnaire and it seems he didn’t want it to end. “It's fun to talk about fatherhood,” he says. Which is good, because he’s got a lot of fathering on his hands right now.

Sources indicate that how's being a twin dad going? I have had friends who were twin parents, and it's so … much.

Overall, it's great. I mean, I think every stage is different. With newborns — it sounds like you're a father as well, so as you know — they're just little potatoes at first. And for the most part, other than the regular feedings and having to wake up multiple times in the middle of the night, which can get tiring, it's not too bad. But obviously those moments … pockets of overwhelmingness of like, "Oh, no." One cries, and then you calm one down, and then another one cries.

Industry observers note that for the most part, I was joking with Natalie, my wife, about it honestly, because you get so nervous about twins. A lot of times when you tell people you're expecting ... People are more prone to just kind of give what I call doomsday advice where it's like, "Oh, get ready for hell," or something like that. And then it happens, and you're so happy and everything feels like a blessing For the most part, it just feels like you got a BOGO, like a buy one, get one free. And it's like, great. Obviously, my wife during the pregnancy, different experience. Obviously, I think it's a lot more on mothers to carry two than one.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that sleep deprivation is a form of torture.
  • Recent findings suggest that as a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I don’t care if I’m reliant on it and you can’t make me.

Sources indicate that sleep deprivation is a form of torture. At some point in every adult’s life, you find out why the hard way. Every parent goes through intense sleep deprivation when they bring home their first baby, and every subsequent newborn after that. But for some of us, sleep never came easy. By the time the babies came on the scene, we were well acquainted with the wee hours of the morning, what it felt like to be up all night, every night.

Recent findings suggest that as a kid, I remember lying in bed for long stretches of time before I could fall asleep. My thoughts would race about everything and nothing. I had a dream catcher above my bed to ward off nightmares, worry dolls under my pillow to whisper my anxieties to so they could “hold them for me” until the morning, and my bedroom TV volume on low while a plucky Disney Channel show played. At sleepovers I was always the last to fall asleep, if I managed to stay overnight at all.

I didn’t get a formal anxiety diagnosis until I went off to college many years later, but learning more about my brain finally gave me an understanding of why sleep was so elusive. With a nervous system stuck in fight-or-flight mode, of course I’d wake at the slightest sound and have a nearly impossible time winding down enough to knock out at the end of the day.

Finally, in 2019, I expressed my frustrations to my latest psychiatrist. I was awake for hours every night waiting for sleep to come, while my husband was already in REM before he ever got fully horizontal on the mattress. I tried guided meditations (why do all the beach ones feature squawking seagulls?) and binaural beats and exercising with the goal of exhausting myself during the day, but my insomnia had reached a frustrating new intensity. It was making my anxiety and depression so much worse; I looked and felt utterly bedraggled. So, he prescribed me trazodone.

Industry observers note that while trazodone isn’t a true sedative — it’s actually an antidepressant — it’s often used off-label to treat insomnia because it gives you a similar relaxing, drowsy feeling. My doctor told me that it’s not a controlled substance and carries a very low risk of addiction, but that mentally, I might start to feel like I need it in order to sleep. If I didn’t like feeling dependent on it, we could make some changes.

“Are they going to stop making it any time soon?” I asked.

“Is it bad to take long-term for any other reason?”.

“Then I’m perfectly fine with being mentally addicted,” I said. And I’ve taken it every single night since then.

In a recent development, research has shown again and again that regularly sleeping well is a key quality-of-life indicator. Lack of sleep negatively impacts every system of the body, weakening the immune system, worsening mental health, and increasing risk of countless conditions, from high cholesterol to Alzheimer’s. Women are twice as likely to have insomnia as men, which has been attributed to our natural hormonal fluctuations throughout the month and the fact that we tend to carry the lion’s share of the mental load in the family, on top of being more prone to mood disorders.

Sources indicate that yet even though we know all of this, taking anything to help you fall asleep is still... kind of frowned upon. Researchers in the UK conducted focus groups interviewing people who take prescription sleep medications and OTC supplements, like melatonin, and found that they had a lot of internalized stigma around the subject — even when talking about it in a room full of people who also take something to help them sleep.

Sources indicate that they found that participants were very deliberate in how they explained their need for their meds. They’re deserving (explaining that their condition, like chronic pain or anxiety, makes sleep impossible without medication). They’re compliant, only ever taking their meds exactly as prescribed (or, in the case of supplements, as directed on the label). They’re responsible, always watching themselves for signs of addiction or misuse. They expressed extreme guilt over taking more of their medications than they should, or trying alternative medications meant to make them sleepy when their usual prescription wasn’t enough.

We recently asked Scary Mommy’s Instagram followers the question, “Do you take anything to fall asleep at night?” Some of that same stigma revealed up in their responses too.

In a recent development, multiple readers remarked they take Gravol when they can’t sleep, calling it a “horrid habit” or something they only do “when things get really bad.” Another said, “I can’t sleep without a quarter of an Ambien. It’s terrible!” “Haven’t had an unmedicated sleep in 7+ years 🫠,” said one response. The melting face is doing a lot of heavy lifting there.

Industry observers note that of course there were plenty of Scary Mommies who felt no shame (that’s sort of our shtick around here). In response to the question “Do you take anything to fall asleep?” one user simply replied, “WINE.” Plenty of other respondents also take trazodone, or Unisom, or some other sleep aid. Weed, whether in vape or gummy form, is also an extremely popular option. See also: a large number of replies indicating they take magnesium and progesterone at night thanks to perimenopause, and that HRT was finally the thing to help them sleep through the night.

But one response really captures my feelings about the whole subject:.

“Oh lord I’m so medicated. But it’s working.”.

Even on the days I feel like I shouldn’t have to take something to help me sleep, that perhaps I could sleepmaxx or wellness hack my way out of having to take a pill every night, I remind myself that not getting enough sleep is literally deadly.

When you’re someone who struggles with sleep night after night, you know how quickly your mental and physical health can plummet. Insomnia decimates my quality of life. Sleep deprivation locks my personality and my joy away behind a concrete wall where I can’t access them anymore. It impacts my longevity and my relationships. While I’m not saying every reader who responded has a healthy way of getting to sleep at night, or that we shouldn’t be critical of our relationships with substances, I think we could all use a little validation that not getting enough sleep is, in fact, torturous.

According to recent reports, more moms need to hear that they deserve to sleep well. They should know that their doctors want to hear from them if they feel abnormally tired during the day. And I want more women to internalize the idea that this world is hard enough to live in as it is. You should at least be able to meet it each day not feeling like a shell of yourself.

And that’s why you can pry my trazodone out of my cold, dead hands.

Nate Bargatze Is (Sort Of) Leading By Example

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.
  • In a recent development, it’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee.
  • Recent findings suggest that but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Though he’s one of the biggest comedians in the world, Nate Bargatze’s career path was anything but straightforward.

In a recent development, it’s a bit hard to believe that Nate Bargatze, one of the biggest comedians today, met his wife while working at Applebee’s in Tennessee. Or that on his first job overseeing the dog kennel in an amusement park (apparently a thing), he let the dog out (“it was a whole thing … and that was kind of the end of the dog kennel”). Or even the basic fact that at the height of his career he decided to move back to Tennessee so that his teen daughter might have a more normal life. Bargatze’s life, like his comedic work, reads like a folksy tall tale. It draws you in with the details and lulls you with its sense of warmhearted authenticity — then lands a punchline.

Recent findings suggest that but authenticity matters to him, in his storytelling and what he’s learned over the years. He recently brought some of his experience to Ford’s Accelerate conference, where he is a spokesperson for what they’re calling the “essential economy” — of skilled technicians and tradespersons, a group that, according to economists, is in short supply and needs to grow. Bargatze is an interesting choice for this forum, a comedian with a high school degree and no formal trade skills besides those he learned onstage. He went to community college for a year and worked a variety of jobs, from waiting at Applebee’s to reading water meters. But he gets the value and opportunity in trade school. “I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools. I did not go to college ... They’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, important for just the future.”.

Nate Bargatze poses with students at the Ford Accelerate conference, which he mc-ed.

He also is thinking about this because his 14-year-old is not too far from entering the workforce. “Right now it’s like, yeah, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it. But then, as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room, so you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to [instill that urgency] as a parent. And if you don’t, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you.” Which all boils down to a most authentic parenting philosophy: “Be a good example, basically.”.

Tell me about what you’re doing right now at this Ford Accelerate event.

It has been revealed that what Ford is doing with this event that we’re at right now, where they’re showing kids going into trade schools ... letting kids know that this is kind of the future, that they’re going to have jobs. And it’s like we don’t know where jobs are going with AI and all this stuff, but the trade schools… We need that. I relate to it very much, because I’m someone that should’ve went to these trade schools.

I worked the water meters. I did not go to college. They’re going to get more college than I did. But they’re going to really learn something and have a craft and know how to do something that is going to be, I believe, vital for just the future. I think they’re putting themselves in such a great position, probably better than they realize now, but they’re going to, I think, look back and just be like, “Man, that was such a good call.”.

I’m wondering, since we’re talking about work, what’s the most important thing you’ve learned about work in your life?

It has been revealed that I always go back to when I waited tables at one point and our manager there always talked about a sense of urgency. And that’s always stuck with me for some reason. It was just going to a table and just have a sense of urgency. It goes a long way when you get to that table and they really feel like they’re being taken care of. I think I’ve just kept that even as I’ve gone forward. If you respond to emails or my team is talking to you, I don’t want to be like, “I’ll get to them next week.” You kind of want to just be like, “No, let’s get to them and let’s make sure that we stay on top of it.”.

Nate Bargatze plays an off-the-rails George Washington when he hosted SNL in 2024.

Speaking of people who don’t have it, how do you instill that sense of urgency in your kid without them fighting back?

It has been revealed that you say stuff as a parent, you don’t know what’s sticking and what’s not sticking. You keep talking about it, and the older she gets — she’s 14 now — the more she’s going to see examples of it. Right now, I don’t know if she’s wrapping her head around it, but then as she continues to get older, she will wrap her head around it. She doesn’t have a sense of urgency of cleaning her room. So you work on that and you just keep saying it and you need to do it as a parent. And if you don’t do it, your kids watch you. So if you don’t have any kind of sense of urgency, they’re going to pick that up from you. And so, be a good example, basically.

Then what’s one thing you wish your kids had today that you had during your childhood?

According to recent reports, I think not the internet, maybe. That would be something, even though it’s great and the connection and it’s all this stuff, you just wish they would’ve had a little more... I think innocence lasted longer when we grew up because you just weren’t pounded with information all day long.

What’s your wife love about you?

According to recent reports, I hope me for being me. We’ve been together before any of this started. We met at Applebee’s. Our 20th wedding anniversary is Oct. 13. I think it’s taking time to get used to it, but we’re along this ride together and just the surprises. We don’t know where everything’s going to end up or what’s going to happen. I think that she sees that I work hard at stuff and has been behind the scenes and loved me before any of this and loves me now. So it’s just to have the support from her, I wouldn’t be here without her. And she very much kept me grounded in a world when you come up in comedy that you could not be... It’s easy to not be grounded.

On the flip side, what do they maybe find annoying about you?

Industry observers note that she doesn’t like eating near me because she thinks I’d chew loud. I don’t think I’m too loud. I think it’s very normal. But she gets very uncomfortable if she’s like... I mean, if she’s on the couch and I’m at the table right behind the couch, she cannot stand it. So I eat outside now — and I only do soups.

Industry observers note that what kind of dad are you? How would you describe yourself as a dad?

It has been revealed that I like to be... You find moments to talk to your kid. As they get older, they have friends. She’s young and all that, so they want to run with their friends. A substantial part is finding the moments of when they can get very talkative, and so you can find these little pockets and really try to home in on those.

She knows I’m a fun time. She can take me for a ride, where her mom can put her foot down a little bit more. She knows where to go. She thinks very much like me, and she can work you if she wants something, and she works me quite a bit.

Coming back to the work thing, what was your first job?

My first job, I worked at Opryland Theme Park in Nashville. I was 15, and so I was a sweeper. I walked around and just swept up the park. And I also did the dog kennel. After the sweeper, I got promoted to dog kennel.

Nate Bargatze with his wife, Laura Bargatze.

Well, because people would bring their pets because they’re on vacation and they’d travel with their pets.

It has been revealed that so you can’t bring them to the park. And so people would bring their dogs in or whatever, their cats. I think we had a chicken. People travel with some weird animals. But one dog got out, and so it was a whole thing. And that was kind of the end of the dog kennel. I think I went back to sweeping after that. But he got out, and so we had to call the... again, pre-internet, so you got to announce to the park, “Whose German shepherd got out in the parking lot?” And then they got to go search for this dog and it was under a parked car. And yeah, I still talk to that family today.

Sources indicate that I’m sure you don’t. They don’t want to talk to you.

In a recent development, no. But I bet they still remember it. We both still remember that.
